Mr. SCHAFFNER presented the second report of the Select Standing Committee appointed to supervise the Official Report of the Debates, as follows:
House of Commons,
Friday, 28th April, 1916.
The Select Standing Committee appointed to supervise the official report of the Debates beg leave to present the following as their second report:
Tour committee have had under consideration the question of the accuracy of the report of a passage in the speech delivered by the Honourable the Minister of Militia and Defence on the 2nd March ultimo, which read as printed:
" There was no quarrel between that gentleman and myself as to who should dictate the patronage. The trouble was that I found something not exactly square and I did not care whether he was Grit or Tory, his head came off."
Tour committee, upon inquiring into the matter, have found that the reporter, in the haste of transcription, accidentally omitted certain words, and that the accurate report, according to the reporter's notes, should read:
"There was no quarrel between me and the other gentleman as to who should dictate the patronage. The trouble was I found the fellow grafting, and when I found something not exactly square, I did not care whether he was Grit or Tory, his head came off."
All of which is respectfully submitted.
(Sgd.) F. D. Schaffner,
,	Chairman.
On the Orders of the Day:

When may we expect
the report of the Commission issued to Sir Charles Davidson to inquire into the purchase of various materials and supplies, , submarines, etc.? It is stated in the newspapers that Sir Charles Davidson has handed a portion of the report to. among others, a clergyman, who was requested to look over it and give his opinion with regard to the purchase of submarines. It the report is ready to be handed out to private individuals, it surely ought to be submitted to this House. I have been told-I do not know how accurate my information is-that Sir Charles Davidson is ready to submit his report, and has offered to submit an interim report to the Government, but there has apparently been no expression of a wish on the part of the Government to have that report. That may or may not be true, but the min-

ister will be able to tell me when we may expect an interim report at least, giving the proceedings to date.

The report is
pretty nearly concluded, and we may expect it to be finished almost any day. I do not suppose my hon. friend would take exception to the course pursued by the commissioner in trying to elicit a^l possible information in reference to a subject in which my hon. friend is interested, the purchase of submarines. In some respects a clergyman ought to be able to give information about such an engine of destruction, but whatever was shown to the clergyman was shown with an idea and a desire to elicit information from the witness in reference to some remarks or strictures that he had passed, based upon newspaper reports, and it was to complete, and to complete on a good basis, the evidence of the witness, that that portion of the report was handed to him. There was nothing improper in that.
Was my hon. friend consulted by the commissioner? He seems to know a great deal.
I take my information from the newspapers, and from some remarks I have heard about the House.

My point was that if
the report is in such a condition that an interim report can be shown to private individuals, it certainly ought to be submitted to this House, because Parliament is the body which is first entitled to receive the report'of the commission and the evidence which has been taken by that commission.

My hon. friend could argue that on the interim report. It was a page of tlhe evidence which was shown to this witness, in order that he might be enabled to sustain or to withdraw or restrict the statement he had made with reference to the transaction, a statement which, I understand, he made on newspaper reports.
On the Orders of the Day:
['I think we had better go into Committee, so that I may finish my statement. I seem to have got one day behind this week.']

Will the Minister of Public Works tell us how the matter stands with regard to the gathering of data in
connection with the supply of water to certain towns from the Saskatchewan river? There was, I think, a commission which undertook to gather data as to the cost, etc., of bringing water from the elbow of the Saskatchewan to different towns, including Regina and Moosejaw. The minister made come public utterance on the matter some time ago.
Mr. ROGER'S: I have not in mind at present the exact standing of the matter,. It has not been up for consideration for some little time, but I will be glad to look it up and give the hon. gentleman any information we have in the department.
On Committee of Supply being called:

Before the House goes into Committee of Supply I propose to make a short statement with reference *to an item which is to be submitted in Committe of Supply-the vote for the administration of affairs under the Canada Grain Act. I do not intend to take up much of the time of the House in doing so, but I have found, in my experience, that when we get into Estimates the committee drifts off into some particular line of controversy, and the Estimates for a most important service may pass through the committee and be finally disposed of while no connected idea of what that service is ie 'brought out by the questioning or is presented to the committee. So that, just for a few moments, I beg the indulgence of the House while I refer to this grain system of ours, which, in a way, is a most wonderful and important development.
When I took charge of the department in 1911, we had the Manitoba Grain Act and part 2 of the Inspection Act, under which the grain business of the West, in so far as it came under the supervision of the Government, was carried out. Besides that legislation, there had been examinations and reports of commissions with reference to a revision or consolidation or reenactment of the Grain Acts so as to bring them more into conformity with the necessities of the situation and with the growth of production in the West. Very valuable information had been gained before that in this way, as I have said, and in 1912 Parliament entered upon the work of perfecting that legislation, and the Canada Grain Act, much as it stands now, was the Tesult of its labours. On the whole,

I think that Parliament was successful, by the co-operation of both sides of the House in a very friendly and frank way, in attaining a * legislation which has stood the test of the four of five years which have passed, and has stood it well. Some more or less important amendments were made to the Act two years ago, and with these amendments the Act stands as it was passed in 1912. Under that Act, from 1911 to the present, a very large development has taken place.
The fundamental feature of that Act, as contrasted with the Act which preceded it, was in placing the administration of the grain system in the hands of a commission, with headquarters at Fort William, instead of, as under the old method, trying to administer the Act from the department here in Ottawa. Three gentlemen were selected who, I think, have justified their choice, and who, from 1911 to the present, have been continuously and busily engaged in the administration of that Act.

I observe that there is no objection on the part of any hon. gentleman to the statement which the hon. minister is making, but I must draw the attention of the House to the fact that there is no motion before it.
I think we had better go into Committee, so that I may finish my statement. I seem to have got one day behind this week.
The House then went into Committee of Supply.

["If on a rising market, neither he nor any one else knows whether the market will rise for another hour. If he does know it, he is, able to go on the market and buy against his belief and make money on the rise. However, I do^not say that it wo.uld be the part of any farmer to go and buy against it. He got the full value of the grain that he had in store the day that it was appropriated, and he got more than that: he got the added value to every bushel that he had behind, and I do not think there were many farmers in western Canada of those who had grain in store who did not have several bushels behind for every one that they had in store. He got the profit that accrued by reason of the increment of value added to what he had left, and he got a fair price for every bushel that he sold. So that, taking it all in all, the farming community of Canada, by virtue of the course taken, were the gainers not by thousands, but by hundreds of thousands-yes, by millions. They would have been gainers also had we taken the other course. The speculators were not by our method losers. On the other hand, they were not the gainers that they would have been if we had taken the course suggested toy hon. gentlemen opposite. They were not the gainers at the expense of our principals, the Allied Commission in Europe. That is what I conceive to be good Government business; that is the course a good Government should pursue. Where it can eliminate the middleman it should do so; where it can act for the benefit of its principals, it should, as any other agent do so faithfully and firmly. That is what we did in this case; we did it to the advantage of the producers and to the advantage of our principals, and they are the parties whose interests we were bound to have in mind.\nAt six o'clock, the House resumed and then took recess.\nThe House resumed at eight o'clock."]

I was going'on to mention the fundamental changes that were made in the legislation passed in 1912, and I was speaking of the formation of the board as one of the chief of those changes. Besides the administration of the Grain Act in the way of licensing, certification, weighing, and inspection generally, power was given to- the board to construct elevators, and under that power action has been taken which will be detailed a little later. So that the Grain Board with its newly constituted powers had something more to do than simply to administer the clauses of the Grain Act referring more particularly to the carriage and inspection of grain.
Under votes of Parliament that have been granted, they have carried out those extraordinary /duties in the construction of a large addition to our storage and

elevator system. Looking at it, as it is now, it seems to me that Canada is one of the best equipped countries in the w'orld, having regard to its population and its general resources. Outside of the United States of America, this is really the foremost country in the world in point of elevator equipment, not only as to capacity for storage, but as to the distribution and situation of the elevators, extending as they do from one coast to the other and being strategically, as it were, placed at the chief points for the reception and shipping of grain. Starting at Halifax, you have a storage capacity, small in extent, of 500,000 bushels; coming to St. John, you have a storage capacity of about
2,000,000 bushels; coming up then to Quebec you have a storage capacity of a little over 1,000,000 bushels; and at Montreal you have a storage capacity of 5,000,000 bushels. Then, you enter upon the large storage - districts of our country, extending through the whole of Ontario, with the great heart and centre at Fort William, then stretching over the Northwest, until finally, at the harbour of Vancouver, the last finished of the series built by the Government is now just about ready for operation. It may surprise the House somewhat-it would one who has not looked into these matters- to know that the total storage capacity for grain in the Dominion of Canada is 172,000,000 bushels, which is a very large proportion of the total grain production of Canada that is liable to come under storage and transit conditions.
Passing from that, which is the general view, we have all kinds of elevators amongst those that I have mentioned. We have the private elevator; we have the hospital elevator for taking care of the sick grain of the country and nursing it back to health and substance again; we have the mill elevator for the convenience of the mills scattered through the country; we have the public elevator and the terminal or transfer elevators at the several ports. The Government elevators form a very considerable part of this whole system. Last year there were inspected of the grain of the country, at Winnipeg, 183,000 cars, amounting to
305,000,000 bushels-, or a little over twice as much as was inspected at Winnipeg in the preceding year. That measures the activity of the grain industry and of the grain transit business through a centre like Winnipeg, which is the great debouching point for grain that is raised in the West, and which will remain so to a large extent, with the exception of what may be taken off

through western exits either towards the far East or via the Panama canal to European markets.
The Government elevator system commenced with the building of the terminal elevator at Fort William. I may say just in passing that the Government-controlled-and-owned elevators have a total capacity of 22,500,000 'bushels, and that those that have been built and are operated under the Grain Board have a capacity of 14,000,000 bushels at the present time. As I have just stated, a big terminal elevator, with, a capacity of 3,250,000 bushels, was^ built at Fort William, and has been in operation now for about three years. In the succeeding year the policy was adopted of having a number of internal storage elevators constructed, and the points that were chosen were Saskatoon, Moosejaw, and Calgary, with transfer port elevators, one at Vancouver and the other at Hudson bay, to be ready for work when that route, if it becomes a grain route to Europe, is opened up. The Government elevators are the most up-to-date of any elevators in the world. They are built on the most approved plans, they are all operated by electricity, they are all equipped with the latest and most effective drying machines, cleaning machines, and apparatus and choppers for the dockage, so as to chop or grind this refuse in a way which will destroy its fecundity land therefor diminish the weed troubles which might arise as it is being used throughout the country as fodder for stock. These Government storage elevators perform the office of furnishing to the people, where they would not otherwise have them in any degree, or to a very limited degree, opportunities for the treatment of grain that becomes damaged, for the cleaning of grain, for the drying of grain, and for the putting into condition the dockage and refuse which is fed to stock.
There is also this added benefit which has arisen from the Government elevators in the interior. Up. to the time of the establishment of these elevators, the farmer at Red Deer, for instance, if he sold his grain, had to wait until that grain found its way to Winnipeg, was inspected there, and the certificate of its grade and weight came back to him at Red Deer. That might consume anywhere from 14 days to a month. In the meantime, he had no document upon which he could go to his bank and get advances on his grain. The fact that at Moosejaw, Saskatoon, and 'Calgary, which are now inspection points, this grain may
be inspected and weighed and almost immediately thereafter the man may get his certificate and may take it to his financial man or bank and get advances upon it, is a very great benefit to the farmer.
In the matter of cleaning, it is surprising to find the quantity of dirt which is carried and paid for, if you sum up the total transit of grain from the place of its production to the ultimate point of its disembarkation. Whatever good arises from the cleansing of grain, in the way of making *it a more saleable product, or in the way of preventing the cost of the carriage of useless material, which accrues to the farmers in the various districts and the producing centres, comes from the facilities which are given by these storage elevators.
These storage elevators, and the terminal elevator, involve an outlay of capital of $5,500,000; or it will be about that when the finishing touches are put upon the Vancouver elevator which, as I have said, is now about ready for work. That expenditure of $5,500,000 has resulted in providing a storage capacity of 14,000,000 bushels, with the incidental advantages of which I have spoken, It is gratifying to know that, as the people come to find what service may be rendered by these Government elevators, they are taking advantage of them. Last year and this year, I think I may say, the revenues which have been derived from the elevators have exceeded by a fairly good amount the expenditures which were necessary in order to have them carried on. The total revenues from the Government elevators last year were a little over $800,000; so that you see the whole matter forms quite an important business in itself.
In order to carry on the operations of that system, the department has, under the Board of Grain Commissioners, about 496 employees at work during the busy season. In 1912, the first year of the operation in the West under the new Grain Act, the number of permanent employees was 79; last year, 1915-16, there were 98; so that there has not been a very large increase in the number of permanent employees when we take into account the fact that whereas in 1912 there was only one elevator, in 1915-16, four elevators were being operated, which of course required a larger force. The increase in the number of employees is of the temporary class, who are employed chiefly during the busy period of the grain season. Under the Grain Commissioners and the Chief Inspector there are detachments of deputy inspectors, samplers, and trackmen, extending all through the sys-

tern; and, if one (fould visualize at any one time in the busy season the work of those men and the tremendous current of grain which passes under their supervision, and every bushel of which has to be inspected, certificated, and weighed, one would get a very pleasing idea of the busyness of the grain industry of the great West and of the country as a whole. These few remarks are all that I intend to make with reference to the general system.
I come now to another point, that is, to explain very briefly what has been asked from the beginning of the session, the commandeering of grain in November last.
I have laid on the table of the House, and the members have it in their possession, a statement which covers all the essential facts; and those who have studied that statement will have the most of the information that I am able to give them this afternoon. The main circumstance which led up to the commandeering of the grain was the very large, and, to a certain extent, abnormal crop of wheat and of oats which was raised in Canada last . year. The Government has been, in the different departments and as a whole, constantly on the alert for every opportunuity to direct the attention both of the British Government and of the allied Governments to the opportunities Which they might have in Canada of providing for themselves those necessaries both as to food and other equipment which they needed for the work and sustenance of the war. This year not only had Canada a very large crop of grain, particularly wheat and oats, but the production of the world was very large. Our neighbours to the south had their bumper crop-a larger crop than had ever before been reaped in the United States. Australia, which the year before had had a failure in her wheat crop, and had been obliged, as also had New Zealand, to im- _ port grain from far-distant countries, Canada included, last year had a bumper crop of wheat, a very large amount of which was available for export. Therefore the Government, in pursuance of its policy of being alive to the necessities of the case and the opportunities that might occur, was especially anxious to call the attention of Great Britain, which had more knowledge of Canada, and of the allied governments of France and Italy, which had not so much knowledge of this country's capabilities, to the possibility of their supplying their wants from Canada and to the advisability of their throwing as much of that
trade as they possibly could into the hands of Canada, which was supporting the war. Not that we wished to be paid m any way for what we were doing in . reference to the war; but, naturally enough, if supplies were to be bought, we urged that due regard should be given to allied countries which were especially well situated to supply certain lines of demand. Negotiations running over two or three months were constantly in hand, and at last on the 23rd of November an order was received, practically from the Allies' commission, but through the British Government, asking the Canadian Government to procure for them a large quantity of wheat. The cablegram was received from the Secretary of State for the Colonies, the Eight Hon. Bonar Law. It is well to remember the date, because nothing could be done towards filling the order until it came to hand. Whatever negotiations were under way, whatever prospects were held out, not a step could be taken to procure a single bushel of grain until the definite order to procure the grain was received.

That order
has not yet been laid upon the Table.

In the memorandum which I laid upon the Table, I mentioned the fact and, I think, the date, and I said to my right hon. friend that the cablegram which covered the order traversed to a certain extent the previous negotiations and covered a wider range than the order, and that it was not thought wise to lay it upon the table of the House, but that if my right hon. friend wished to see it I would -be very glad to let him peruse it. That is the way in which that matter stands at the present time.
Would the minister have , any objection to giving us now his summary of the purport of the cablegram which constituted the order, eliminating those parts which have nothing to do with it?
The purport of the order, in so far as it affects Canada and the purchase of wheat by Canada, can be summed up in a very few words. It was an order to purchase a very large quantity of wheat.
A given quantity?

'The given quantities which were to be bought at that time were preceded by negotiations which looked towards other quantities, and this first

purchase was as a commencement and, in one way, as a reserve to be drawn upon as it was needed; so that the meaning and significance of the order, looking to preceding negotiations, was that we were authorized immediately to commence purchasing. There was the desire not only to have the grain purchased, but to geit it just as quickly as possible. The urgency of the order together with the date at which it came, the 23rd of -November, made it necessary for the iGiovernment to act quickly. The 23rd of November brings you pretty close to the very active season of shipping, pending the -close of navigation on the lakes. The Government had to decide how the purchase should be made.
Right here let -me say frankly and decidedly that the British Government did not dictate to the Canadian Government any method to be employed in procuring that grain,-I suppose they never thought of such a thing. All we were asked to do was to purchase the grain. There are three ways in which the grain might have been purchased. Judging from remarks I have heard in the House it seems to have been thought by some, -and it may be thought still, that the better way would have been to have gone to the West and buy direct from the individual farmers the grain that was required. I think a little consideration will make it clear that that would not have been a wise method to pursue. In the first place, it was not possible. We could not have sent to the farmers of the West a number of buyers and by any possibility have got the grain to Fort Willia-m before the closing of lake navigation; and that, if there were no other consideration, precluded the adoption of that method of purchase. Another method of purchase was to select brokers and have them buy on the grain exchanges the amount required, some 12,000,000 bushels more or less. The first objection to -that is that you pay a large commission. The Government was in the place of the purchaser and to a large extent trustee for the purchaser, and, consequently, it was its duty to buy the grain at the very best possible price.
Did the order convey any statement as to price?

Nothing. Then, as to the use of brokers; if the business had been done through only one broker difficulty would have arisen, and if more-than one broker had been employed competition would have arisen. The moment a government begins to purchase grain on the exchanges, no matter how secretly, there is telepathic connection which makes the information common in a very short time, and then the knowledge that the Government is purchasing and that brokers' are competing for gram for the Government causes an increase in the price and may lead to a very large increase. A year before this operation, European governments commenced buying grain in Canada and the United States. They bought openly. As a result the market went wild and the prices rose rapidly, away beyond any actual value. Those prices, of course, could not be maintained, but they were very uneconomical and expensive to the countries that were buying. 'Taking these things into consideration, and after having taken the best advice they could get and- studying the question for what time was allowed them- for there was not much time left-the Government came to the conclusion that the fairest way all round was to take possession of the grain by commandeering it. As a result of their decision, on the 27th of the month they sent an order to the Government elevators at Fort William and the public elevators- in eastern Canada and the Government-controlled elevators, to retain all wheat in store at that hour, of the grades of No. 1, No. 2, and No. 3, and reserve it for the use of the Government. That was done, and as a result 10,300,348 bushels of these grades was commandeered at the head of the lakes and 3,321,458 bushels in the eastern elevators, a total of 13,621,806 bushels. The price which was current on the day when the commandeering order passed was the price paid for that grain, $1.04} for No. 1 Manitoba, and proportionate prices for No. 2 and No. 3. The market before that had been on the upgrade, not violently, but -still upwards. That being the case, I think we are justified in concluding that every man whose grain was taken stood to lose nothing on the mon-ey he had invested in the grain. If he were not a speculator, if he were not holding for a profit, if he were disposed to be just the seller for the day, -he received a fair and equitable price for his grain. He had an honest price, whether he got a speculative price or not. There is this- consideration also, that -the grain which was bought was held mainly by middlemen. Had the Government gone on the market and bought grain from day to day at ascending prices, the man who bought the

grain at lower prices would, have been the one to profit by the increased price brought about by the purchase. But, in commandeering, that state of affairs cannot obtain; you commandeer and you have the grain on the instant and at the current price of the day. After the buying of a large quantity of grain by the Government, even by the commandeering process, the idea gets abroad that possibly more will be bought. In any case, a very large quuantity has been taken out of the market and out of the hands of the holders, and these people must go back to the primary source, to the farmer, to replenish the store. Then, whatever increase in price takes place in commandeering, or shortly after, while the re-purchase is going on, redounds to the benefit of the producer, or primary holder, that is, to the farmer himself. I grant that difficulties have to be met, and would have had to be met under any form of purchase; but, taking all things into consideration, I believe that the method followed was the best for the Allies. They got the grain at the current rate of that day, at one equable and honest price, and had to pay nothing by way of increased valuation which would have taken place if the grain had been bought on the instalment plan from da]^ to day on rising prices. So that the Government performed its duty as trustee of the allied nations by getting the grain for them without paying a commission price, at the current rate of the day, and without the risk of any increasing prices which might be due to the buying of grain by the Allies in the market.
An additional reason why haste was a factor in the arrangement when that grain was commandeered was that as much as possible of the grain, should, in the interests of the allied nations, be got out before the freezing up of the lakes and at the cheapest possible rate of carriage. That also was a factor in determining the Government to commandeer the grain. When the grain was commandeered, difficulties arose: we knew that they would arise; but it was possible to mitigate those difficulties. The first difficulty was this: if 10,000,000 bushels of grain taken by the Government, which was in store at the head of the lakes awaiting an x opportunity to utilize the short period of lake transit which was left to it before the closing of navigation, had/remained in the hands of the Government, any person who had wished after that date to take advantage of lake transit 
would have had to commence by a repurchase, which on the most rapid arrangement would have made him late by days ' and perhaps by weeks in getting to Fort William and making ready for transit by the lakes. Some method, therefore, had to be arranged by which there should not be a stoppage of the outflow of the grain by the lakes for the limited period of lake traffic that remained. That difficulty was got over in a way that is usual at Fort William and at such places. The grain commissioners loaned that grain to those who had vessels in readiness and who wished to get their grain out to the United States lake ports or to the eastern lake ports of Ontario, keeping the bill of lading, a perfect security, under the condition that the grain was to be replaced within ten days. Some 7,500,000 4 p.m. bushels were thus loaned, and from the morning of the day after the commandeering when that system was adopted, to the night of Tuesday,
10,000,000 bushels took water at Fort William-a record output in the history of the lake ports. No barrier, therefore, was opposed to the quick and ready transit of grain by the only water route which was available for a short period of time. Every bushel of this grain was restored and got into transport condition at the head of the lakes within ten' days from the time that the loan was made. Thus was that difficulty overcome.
The next difficulty that arose was this: Nearly all the eastern millers of Ontario had grain in the eastern elevators or at Fort William-almost entirely in the eastern elevators-which they expected to get quickly by the lake route in order to keep their mills going. The mills do not hold much in reserve. Indeed, many of them hold scarcely anything in reserve; they hold 'it in the elevator and take it out from day to day or from week to week as they require it. When this grain in the eastern elevators was commandeered the supply of the mills was entirely cut off. In order to keep the mills supplied with grain and to provide against the closing of the mills, many of which were engaged on contracts for flour for the allied Governments, we adopted this arrangement; we unconditionally released all grain that was commandeered in the eastern elevators, upon the deposit with the Government of a guarantee by the millers that the grain had been' bona fide contracted for and that it was to be ground

up in their mills and used for no other purpose. We released about 1,900,000 bushels of grain from the commandeer; that grain went into the hands of the millers, and the millers' operations went on just the same as if there had 'been no commandeer. This provided for that difficulty. It reduced the total quantity of commandeered grain by that amount.; but you could not go into these elevators and commandeer a portion of the grain; you had to commandeer the whole, and the total commandeer was a little more than was necessary for the supply of the allied nations for the months of December and January.
How much would have actually supplied the requirements of the Allies for the two months that my hon. friend mentions?
I could not tell my hon. friend how much. Purchases are still being made on account of the Allies.
By the Government?
No,, not by the Government.
The minister referred to two specific months, and said that a certain amount was too much.
I did, because certain quanti ties were to be delivered each month.
Did this commandeered grain leave the country by Canadian ports?
I will come to that in the course of my narrative.

I think the answer to that is very easy. Before a single ship could be sent or ordered to be sent to an Atlantic port, there had to be a certainty that the grain would be there for it when
it came, and it was impossible to buy grain and send it down to the seaboard in driblets. It was absolutely necessary that there should be a certainty of an ample supply of grain in order that the Allies might intelligently arrange for its transportation. It is true that 7,500,000 bushels were loaned out of the Fort William elevators, and loaned for a period the utmost limit of which was 10 days; but that was not subversive in the least .of the system which the Allies would put. into operation for-carrying their grain. Even if, on the day of the commandeer, and when a cablegram went that so much grain 'had been secured, the Allied Governments had been able to send ships out, the ships could not have reached Atlantic ports before the return of the grain that had been loaned and its gradual movement to the Atlantic seaboard. The difficulty that arose was along this line: Bona fide contractors, with the Old Country purchasers for grain, found that by this commandeer the grain which they had contracted for with those purchasers, and for the transport of which cargo space had been taken-and the cargo space itself was coming across the ocean and must be met here-could not be procured, and that, if the commandeer remained upon that grain, and there was no condition under which they could fulfil their contract except by going back to the West, purchasing a new supply, and bringing it down to the seaboard, much of it necessarily having to come by rail, it would have been quite impossible, in many cases, for them to have carried out their contracts on time, and the vessels would have had to wait in port to be loaded, with heavy demurrage. The arrangement made to overcome that difficulty was this: To the man who had a bona fide contract with British purchasers and who showed the evidence of that contract, we released the quantity of grain required to fill that contract, and he gave us his undertaking and deposited his guarantee that he would return that grain, in store, at a certain time. Under that arrangement no difficulty of any moment arose with reference to the bona fide contract men who were exporters of Canadian grain to the British market. Some trouble and some confusion was no doubt caused; but at the same time I must say, in justice to both grain holders and grain buyers, in Winnipeg, in Montreal, in Toronto, all along the line, that, although they would have preferred that the commandeer had not taken place, they took it in good spirit.

They fell in with our plans and did not object very strongly. There was, on the whole, a hearty co-operation with the Government in the carrying out of the arrangements that made it possible for them to keep their contracts.
'The minister said the grain was loaned to people having contracts. What was the limit of the time for which it was loaned ?

That grain was to be returned at different dates, and those dates were, as nearly as possible, arranged in connection with our knowledge of the possibility of vessels coming to receive it, and being able to get here at certain dates.
Did all of that gram have to be returned before tbe close of navigation?

No. Very little of the export grain could be returned before navigation closed. That grain would have to be returned after navigation closed, and returned in store at Fort William, which was done. So that those three arrangements which I have tried to explain, carried out in connection with the commandeer, caused the least possible confusion and derangement of the grain trade, and, on the whole, I think it has worked out exceedingly well.
I know that some criticisms will come. One criticism will be founded upon a question which will be .asked:	Has all of this
grain gone out yet? I answer to that: No. Then the further question will be asked: Why were you in such a hurry to get the grain on the 27th day of November if it has not all been carried out up to this date? This much I shall say, that there has been always more grain ready for loading than could be carried by the ships provided by the Allies to transport it from our ports; and the balance of the grain will probably not leave our ports before the middle of May, when the last of it will be taken out from the port of Montreal. Just about the time of the commandeering of the grain, the difficulty of obtaining tonnage for the Allied powers for the operations of the war and other operations subsidiary to them became acute; and, although Italy, one of the allied powers, was in great need of that grain, in dire need of it-because Italy, before the war had been declared, had carried on a very brisk trade with Germany and had sold a large propor-

tion of her wheat to Germany, so that when the war was declared between Italy and Germany-Italy came into the war-

Italy and Austria. Italy
is not at war with Germany.
Anybody can sleep on that who wishes. It does not appear to me that they are very friendly with each other.

They could
buy and sell though.

In a technical
point of view, no war has been declared. That is true. But, in the other point of view, Italy is doing her level best to destroy the cause of the Teutonic Allies, and doing it with a bravery and a consistency that has not been excelled by any nation which has been engaged in the war. So that, intervening, was this extreme scarcity of tonnage; and, although there has been necessity for the quickest possible transit of that grain, it has been impossible for them to provide the vessels necessary more speedily than they have done. Three-fourths of that grain has already left tbe Atlantic seaports, and probably a little more than one-fourth remains yet to be taken out. Now, I think that is all the statement I have to make with reference to the commandeering.
For whose benefit was the wheat bought?

As I think my statement shows, the wheat went into the hands, of the Allied Commission in London. That is a commission on which representatives from Italy and Russia and France and Great Britain sit. There may be some others on it, but these are the principal representatives, and they are under the presidency, or chairmanship, of a British official. That Allied Commission purchases supplies of every kind necessary for the war, or for the sustenance of the people en-' gaged in the war. They have their methods of finance arranged in conjunction with Great Britain, and they sit there as a commission, receive bids, make contracts, and make purchases., and they d* this in common session. The moment that the grain commandeered was in out possession it was handed over, at exactly the cost and charges that were incurred, to this Allied Commission, and from that time it has been under their charge as to its disposal. They asked the Department of Trade and Com-

meroe to undertake the supervision of that grain from the point where we procured it to the seaboard, and to see that it met the ships at the different ports. My department undertook that supervision and has been carrying it out.
Are these Canadian ports?

They are not all Canadian ports. Wherever the Allied Commission, which is providing the vessels, could get a vessel to go most conveniently and most economically, they asked us to send the wheat, and this wheat has been provided and loaded at ports from Baltimore in the South to Halifax and St. John in the North.	'
The commission has purchased also in the United States.
Has this commission purchased any wheat in Canada besides what the Government purchased for it?

I think I may
say that before that time, and since that time, the countries represented on, that commission have purchased in Canada, and purchased very largely.

I see by the correspondence brought down that France purchased direct in Canada without the intervention of this commission. I know- it is public knowledge-that the Allied Governments have been purchasing largely in Canada. What I want to know is whether that commission has purchased in Canada from private parties in addition to what was purchased through the Government.
Yes, the commission has purchased, and is purchasing.
Is this the only occasion oh which the Government was called upon to commandeer?

My hon. friend must not put it' in that way; he must not say that the Government was called upon to commandeer. The Government was no$ called upon to commandeer; it was called upon to purchase. Commandeering was resorted to a year ago, or a little more, 202
when a quantity of oats was secured in that way for the French and British Governments, I think.

The action
taken by the Government in the month of November last, at the end of the season,, was absolutely exceptional, and no such action should (be taken by a government except under exceptional circumstances. A government should not interfere so as to dislocate trade in any way, or to raise an obstacle to the ordinary channels of trade unless there is an absolute necessity for doing so. iSo far as my information goes, and I think it is perfectly accurate-it is within the knowledge of everybody-no government anywhere ever commandeered any commodity except for the purpose of immediately supplying the people for consumption. There may, perhaps, foe circumstances where a different course has been pursued, but, as a rule, no commandeering of any commodities ever took place in any country unless there was a possibility of famine in the particular commodity, and the government saw that the people were suffering. In this instance, the Government received information, as my hon. friend says, on the 23rd of November last that the Allied Nations were wanting wheat. In the statement which he places before the House my hon. friend proceeds- as follows:
Early in the autumn of 1915 when it became evident that Canada, in common with the United States and Australia, would have large surpluses of wheat for export, representations were made to the British Government with a view of interesting it and the Allied Governments in the purchase from Canada of a generous portion of the large quantities they would undoubtedly require.
That was certainly a very commendable action on the part of the Government-to try to enlist at once the good-will of the Allied Nations and to see that they supplied themselves in Canada with a commodity of which we had a large surplus. Then my hon. friend goes on to say:
These representations were successful and on November 23, instructions were cabled to the Canadian Government by the Secretary of State for the Colonies to purchase a large quantity, delivery to begin in December and continue for the following months.
It would have been sufficient to draw the attention of the Allies to the fact that we had a very large crop in Canada, and then to leave the ordinary channels of trade to supply the necessities of the Mother Country and the Allied nations. The Government, however, thought they would go into the business themselves; they became pur-



chasers of wheat for the benefit of the Allied nations, and the result of their efforts was to secure . the magnificent quantity of 13,000,000 bushels. That was all they could do or all that they attempted to do. When there was a surplus available for sale of at least 100,000,000 bushels of wheat in the month of November, my hon. friend, by the method he adopted, secured 13,000,000 bushels. Was there any necessity for that action? What purpose was served, or what benefit accrued to anybody from it? What reason was there for dislocating trade, as it was dislocated at the moment-so much so that two days afterwards my hon. friend was obliged to see that that man got his quantity and that other man got his quantity, that the shippers got their quantity, and the millers their quantity-what was the reason for such action if the object could have been accomplished just as effectively by the ordinary methods of trade, winch would have been far better than the the extraordinary methods followed by the Government. My hon. friend has attempted to justify himself, and I do not think that he has made out a case at all for resorting to this extraordinary process. He said that the wheat was bought without any commission, but every purchaser is prepared to pay commission where the ordinary methods of trade are followed, and there is no reason at all why the ordinary methods of business, which are legitimate, should not have been followed. There is no reason why. The only excuse for it is that it was a case of necessity. My hon. friend is aware that at the time this extraordinary, this despotic, action was taken by the Government, there were serious complaints coming from all over Canada from men in the business that the Government were interfering with their legitimate operations, and up to this day I have not heard a single good reason why this extraordinary action of the Government was taken. I submit that there was no excuse for the Government to interfere, and that these operations should have been left to the trade. At the very moment when my hon. friend was taking this extraordinary action, the French Government, as appears from the correspondence which my hon. friend has brought down, was a purchaser of grain in Canada, and my non. friend seized part of the grain which belonged to the French Government, and which had been purchased on their behalf by the Hudson Bay Company. Was there any reason 
why my hon. friend should not have employed either the Hudson Bay Company or other operators rather than by arbitrary action to take hold of the grain that was on the lakes and in the hands of the operators at that time? Whilst in times of war we are not disposed to be critical, at the same time I submit very sincerely that there was no justification whatever for such action.
There is another thing: I do not see why the whole of the correspondence has not been brought down. My hon. friend knows the rule of this House, that if a public document is quoted it must be laid on the Table. My hon. friend said that there were some parte of the correspondence that were confidential. Anything that is confidential I do not ask for, but what is not confidential should have been brought down for the information of thp House. That is the rule that has always been followed. The whole of the correspondence has not been brought down. I see by the return that an Order in Council was passed on the 4th December last. This order in council was afterwards cancelled and was replaced by another one which is in these terms:	,
The minister further reports that the action which he has taken for the above purpose is set forth in the telegrams, copies of which are hereto appended, and that the instructions given in the messages signed by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, the Minister of Railways and Canals and the' Solicitor General were sent after consultation witji him and at his request in pursuance of the proposed appropriation and control of the wheat aforesaid.
The last paragraph of this Order in Council, which was passed on the 8th December, is in these words:
The minister recommends that the Order in Council P.C. 2873, respecting the appropriating of wheat, passed on the 4th day of December, 1915, be repealed.
That is to say, they first passed an Order in Council on the 4th December, and four days afterwards, on the 8th December, this Order was repealed and replaced by the one to which I have alluded. The first Order in Council was not brought down. I suppose it is not very material, but still the order of the House was to bring down all the correspondence, and in this the order of the House has not been carried out. Then, here is something that appears to be very strange. There is another Order in Council pas'sed on the 8th January, in which it is stated that the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Finance recom-/

mend that " in order to in part effectuate the provisions of the Order in Council of the 4th December, 1915, ratifying the appropriating " of wheat and so on, a certain disposition be taken. But the Order in Council of the 4th December had been already repealed. On the 8th January, in order to effectuate the Order in Council of December 4, an Order in Council is passed, notwithstanding the fact that the Order in Council of December 4 had been repealed. I just make these comments, because it seems to me that the whole thing is very irregular. Whilst I am not disposed to insist upon the irregularity of the proceeding, still it is a thing which ought not to be repeated. The last statement made by my hon. friend showed that there was absolutely no necessity for the proceeding. He acted suddenly, saying there was great necessity for having it done immediately. The purchase was made on the 27th November, before the close of navigation, but the wheat had not all been delivered to the allied nations that purchased it.
That is so.
Then where was the necessity?
I anticipated that criticism, and I have answered it.

What is the
answer?
When my right hon. friend finishes, his remarks I will answer him.

Now he gives us the excuse that it was impossible to secure tonnage to expedite the shipments. Everybody knows that, but if my hon. friend had not the tonnage to expedite shipment there was no necessity for any such hurry to commandeer the wheat. If there was to be any benefit to anybody on account of the condition of the wheat market, certainly the vendors, the producers, were entitled to it.

I have no fault to find with the remarks of my right hon. friend in the way of criticism at this moment, not in the least. If 'he had been leading a government at that time, and the circumstances had developed exactly as they did, and it had come to the point where action, was necessary, be might not have had acted in the same way that this Government did, but his Minister of Trade and Commerce might have adopted a dif-
