ferent method of procuring action along the lines which he has. indicated would have been best, and might not have taken the method which we took. It is simply a question of the judgment of the purchasing authority-the Government in this case- as to the conditions at the time of the purchase and the necessities of the case. Upon the conditions as they were, and the necessities of tiie case, this Government came to the conclusion that they must get that gTain and get it at once, because it was necessary to have it.
I will take up in order what has been stated by my right hon. friend by way of objection. First, he said that commandeering should never !be resorted to as a general rule, and has never been resorted to, except in the ease of some great necessity in the country itself, such as lack of food, where privation, if not starvation, must ensue unless the Government commandeers, takes hold of, and feeds out gradually and by Tation, as it were, what is necessary to prevent such privation or starvation from taking place. But there are other circumstances in which, upon the very same principle, commandeering might take place. I have mentioned the condition of Italy m reference to the shortage of wheat. The shortage of wheat in Italy at that time was absolutely acute. The information was before the Government that Italy needed a certain quantity of wheat, as much or more than tihe wheat which was* commandeered, and that they needed it absolutely at that time. There was no bargain that the Government here was to prepare or supply the tonnage which should carry the wheat. The necessity was there. Italy and the other allied Governments were to look after the wheat being carried, and at the time that order was given the expectation here was-ana no other expectation could have been formed under the circumstances.- that that quantity of wheat was absolutely necessary, would be called for, and would be taken out of the country within a very short time. Now, what I have stated,
I think, is absolutely plain and fair. What I stated was that acute scarcity of tonnage supervened, which made it impossible for the Italian Government, with the aid of the British Government and the Allied Governments, to get sufficient ships to carry that wheat out at once, and Italy's needs had to be and were to a certain extent met by going to another market and getting what she wanted from another source.
When was the wheat shipped to Italy and how much was shipped ?
Wheat has been shipped ever since and is being shipped now.
Was any wheat shipped to Italy say, within six weeks after the commandeering took place?
I do not think there was.
DV the commandeering of the wheat we did not assist any dire need in Italy, because Italy would have been in need yet so far as the action of this Government is concerned.

My hon. friend may think that is a criticism, but I hardly agree with him. If we had known everything, if we had known that this intervention of scarcity of tonnage' would take place and that the Italian Government would not be able to get the tonnage to send for the wheat when we expected them to send for it and to get it, and if we had acted upon that knowledge, then we could have .taken our time and have procured the wheat from time to time and in driblets.

I do not wish to interrupt the minister, but it seems to me that if the commandeering of the supply of wheat was such an absolutely urgent matter at that time, it would have been an easy matter foT the Government to ascertain whether there were available vessels in which to take that wheat out.

It was not the duty of this Government to find the vessels. When an order comes for wheat and when there is urgency for that order, you fulfil it under the circumstances and conditions as they are at the time. If something intervenes so that the shipping cannot be found, and the wheat cannot be sent forward, that comes afterwards; it is not within the knowledge of the purchasing party at the time the purchase is made.
May I ask a question?

Will you allow me to go on until I answer the objections of my Tight hon. friend ? I will take his question after I get through. He must always give way to his leader.
My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition says every purchaser is 
prepared to pay a commission. He argued that the consideration that this wheat got in that way would not have to cost more to the Allied Governments was not a tenable one, because every one who purchased knew that a commission was to be paid. Weil, I would not like to say that in cases of war necessity- and this was war necessity-it is good doctrine that, even if you <jan get wheat at a lower price by paying no .commission, it is still well to adhere to the course of trade and pay a commission. My right hon. friend is on dangerous ground when he presses an argument of that kind.
My right hon. friend says that the Order in Council of the 4th of December was not brought down. There is no objection to its being brought down. After the Order in Council was passed, it was found to be defective in certain respects, and instead of passing an ordeT just to amend that Order in Council, and leave them both with efficacy, the Government thought that the best w(ay, as is often done, was to embody the first Order in Council in the second, with the amended portions, and pass the one Order in Council covering the whole thing. I will give my right hon. friend the first Order in Council at any time if he thinks it is necessary to have it.
Then, he made a statement with reference to the Order in Council of January 8 being based on the Order in Council of December 4, which was cancelled. Perhaps that may be technically a ground for criticism, but the Order in Council of December 4 was virtually in and formed the substance of the amended Order in Council which was passed on December 8, The Order in Council of January 8, was, I think, largely for the purpose of financing the whole arrangement. If my right hon. friend would like to know what the arrangement was, I may say that a credit was opened with the Bank of Montreal, which advanced the money necessary to pky for this wheat as the payments fell due, that the Government stood behind that loan as a guarantor of it, and that the whole of that amount has already and long since been paid off.
Now, if my hon. friend from Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) has a question? Maybe my hon. friend wants to make a speech instead of to ask a question.

I will surprise my hon. friend by not making a speech. I would like to know who initiated the whole business? Did the proposition start from this

Government or on a request from the Old Country?

I have already
answered that half a dozen times, I think. I said as plainly as a man could say that the British Government never indicated to this Government how it should procure that wheat-whether it should buy it under commission, buy it by an agent or broker, go to the farmers and buy it direct, or how it should buy the wheat. Our order was simply to procure the wheat for them, and this Government takes the whole responsibility of the method it took to procure the wheat.

I did not ask the minister- with regard to details of that kind. The minister was proceeding to say that it was none of the business of this Government how the wheat could get to Italy. I thought it was an opportune time to ask him who first opened negotiations looking towards this Government being the instrument of getting the wheat across. Did this Government take the first step towards facilitating the supplying of wheat, or did the request come from the Old Country because of the dire need of Italy, and so on?

I think my hon. friend must have that information. The whole action was based upon the statement that with the supply that we had the Government was anxious to direct all possible purchases of wheat to this country; and from the time the crop began to be garnered until the order came we were in constant communication with reference to supplying not only wheat but other supplies and necessaries to the Allied Governments; and you may say if you like that the suggestion came from this Government to the Allied Governments asking them sympathetically to consider all possible purchases of supplies from Canada, and that after negotiations had gone on for a certain time in respect to this and many other things, this order came for the purchase of wheat.
Has fault been found with the minister for not having commandeered more wheat when he was at it?

I do not know. Fault may have been found in a great many ways. That has not come particularly to my mind, although I do recollect now, when my hon. friend mentions it, that some persons were strongly in favour of our commandeering the whole western crop.

I thought my right
hon. friend was in favour of it.

My hon. friend has favoured the House with a speech in two parts, one dealing with the question of elevator accommodation and the actions of the Grain Commission for the Government's handling of the grain trade generally, and the second part dealing with the details of the commandeering, of wheat last fall, which is probably one of the most controversial matters that could be brought up in the House of Commons. The whole question of the Government's handling of the grain trade of Canada is necessarily important in the last degree, and, being important, is necesarily controversial. If I take the opportunity of criticising the policy of the Government and its administration in regard to its handling of the grain trade generally, I hope it will not be said that I am doing so particularly from partisan motives.
Not at all.

It is desirable that there should be a clear understanding as to whether the policy pursued by the Government is the best policy or not the best policy, and, as some of us hold differing views, it is our duty to place those views before the country.
The minister epoke of the amount of elevator accommodation in Canada and expressed the opinion that very satisfactory conditions exist in this country in regard to the transportation and handling of grain. He said we were probably the best-situated country in the world in this respect, at any rate next to the United States. He said that we have a splendid system of handling grain, one of our advantages being that grain is handled under the Grain Commission and in part through elevators which are the property of the Government and are under the control of the commission. This, of course, brings up the question whether the Government has used the best judgment in the interests of the country in its location of the elevators, in the expenditure of money upon these elevators, and generally the results of their policy to the producers of the grain. I apologize for introducing a matter so controvei'sial, but it is necessary that we should know where we are at in this matter. I am compelled, therefore, to recall to attention the fact that before the present Government took office, in the contest which resulted in their taking office, it
Who spread it?
Newspapers supporting my hon. friend.
Not one of them. Has the hon. gentleman a quotation?
It is a fact; there is no argument by which-
It is not a fact.
Yes, it is.
Oh, no.

My hon. friend had better not butt in; he has not been doing himself much good by that lately. A plain fact is a plain fact. I am not holding the Government directly responsible. I am not saying that the Government put it in the Canada Gazette, but I am saying that newspapers supporting this Government did spread that idea broadcast, and I cannot think that they did it without having some indication from the Government that warranted them in doing it. To such an extent was that idea spread-my hon. friend will not deny this-that the British Board of Trade cabled to Canada to deny that the British Government had anything to do with the commandeering of that wheat.
Does the hon. gentleman know for a fact that that was cabled?

Certainly: it became necessary for the protection of the good name of the Government of Great Britain for the Board having authority in the matter to cable to this side of the water to deny that they were responsible for that action. It may seem a light thing to my hon. friend to interfere with the business that relates to agriculture when it seems such a tremendous thing to interfere with the business of shipping, or nickel, or any of these other matters. But I want to say-and this is why I am speaking so strongly- that inasmuch as the agricultural industry is the principal wealth producing industry in this Dominion of Canada, it not only is entitled to every advantage that this Government can give it in the way of administration, but it is entitled not to be interfered with in any detrimental way unless the gravest reasons can be brought forward for that interference, no such reasons having been brought forward in this particular case.
It was most unfortunate that this seizure of wheat at Fort William should have been made within the last few days preceding the close of navigation. The minister has said that it was because the close of navigation was so near at hand that it became necessary to seize the wheat. Well, if it was necessary to seize the wheat because the end of the season of navigation was near, it was necessary that the seizure should have remained on that wheat and that the seized wheat should have gone forward while navigation was open. But, inasmuch as the wheat seized was, in

large proportion, afterwards released, his argument that it was necessary to seize because the close of navigation was approaching falls absolutely to the ground. He said that during the few days following the seizure a larger amount of grain took water at Fort William than during any similar period in the history of the country. That is probably true; but it is also true that there was either one or two days when grain did not take water. There were only 8 or 10 days in which grain could take water, and the seizure of the grain held up that grain for that time. Much more grain would have taken water had the seizure not taken place. The minister rested his case practically on the near approach of the close of navigation. That was the chief reason why it was necessary to seize instead of buying-in order to get the summer outlet for the grain. But dong after navigation closed, as the Minister of Railways told us the other night, the Government itself, over its own railroad, gave a rate on grain to Montreal absolutely identical with the summer rate. Thus the minister is left without a shadow of a ground of reason for seizing the grain at the time he did. The grain could have been bought at any time, and could have been brought forward at any time during the whole winter at exactly the same rate as it was being shipped out at Fort William on the day it was seized. There was therefore no reason why that grain should not have been bought in the ordinary coUrse of trade, so far as facilities for bringing it forward or the cost of transportation was concerned. In the ordinary way it would have reached its ultimate destination. As a matter of fact it has not yet -reached its destination, although the course of trade was interfered with.
When in- Winnipeg recently I asked a gentleman connected with the Grain Exchange what estimate was placed on the losses of dealers owing to the disarrangement of the market. He said the amount was variously estimated, but that the minimum was $200,000 of direct loss to the men engaged in the grain trade in Winnipeg and the western country owing' to the action of the minister. I ask the minister if he thinks it was right to disarrange 'the trade of our country to an extent sufficient to' cause a loss of $200,000 to men who my hon. friend says were speculators. Well, they were speculators; there is no doubt about that. So is every man who buys a stock of groceries and puts it into his store and sells it out again. The grain

trade of Canada and of the world is carried on by speculators. They are just as necessary a part of the grain business of our country as the elevators or the railroads or as my hon. friend's grain commissioners. There must be men to buy and sell grain or grain will not be bought and sold, and when the minister lightly suggests that because it was grain dealers who lost the $200,000 it is a matter of no concern to the people of the country, I can only say I cannot agree with him. The grain trade is in the hands of the grain dealers in large measure; just as the Grain Commission controls the direction of the trade in a certain way, just as the railroads carry the grain and the elevators handle it, so the grain dealers are the men through whose hands it passes.

I understood the hon.
member to say that the grain commandeered was owned by the farmers who had shipped it to Fort William in cars. The hon. member now says that the bulk of the grain was owned by grain dealers and not by the farmers.

I do not wish to be understood as having said that the grain commandeered belonged to the farmers. I was speaking of the general situation. That is a matter with which I shall deal later. The grain crop goes through the hands of the grain dealers. If the grain dealers dropped $200,000 by reason of the interference of the Government, they will see that they are insured against any further contingency of that kind by taking it' out of the farmer in any future business transactions. As a matter of fact, the hon. member for Q'Appelle (Mr. Thomson) pointed out this session that since the grain was commandeered there has been a greater spread between the track and street prices than before, simply because the dealer was insuring himself against any further interference by the Government in the transactions of the grain trade.
Then the speculator did not lose. That proposition has gone by the board.	'
The speculator says he did lose. Part of the grain that was in the elevators at Fort William and that was seized belonged to the farmers, part of it to the millers, and part of it to dealers.
In about what proportions ?

I understand that about 3,000,000 bushels belonged to the farmer*. That was grain that had been shipped to Fort William in car lots by the farmers who produced it. It is a remarkable fact that it was 3,000,000 bushels that was held by the Government. Nearly 2,000,000 bushels was returned to the millers and seven and a half million bushels was returned to the dealers, but 3,000,000 bushels was held by the Government-the 3,000,000 bushels that belonged to the farmers.
Surely.

Surely. And on the 3,000,000 bushels that belonged to the farmers the farmers lost the benefit of the advance in price to which they were entitled, and which they would have received if the Government had not seized their wheat. The Government loaned back to the dealers and back to the millers, 'but they did not loan back to the farmers.

Was that all the wheat they had?
(Mr. OLIVER: No.
Then, why did they not sell the other wheat?

The reason why they did not sell all their wheat was that the Government did not facilitate the transfer of that wheat to the Atlantic seaboard. They have the wheat on their hands yet, but not that particular 3,000,000 bushels. It is a remarkable fact that the amount of wheat which the Government held synchronized with the amount of wheat which the farmers had in the elevators, and while the handling of the grain of the miller and the grain " dealer was facilitated, the farmer simply lost without recourse, and he has no recourse yet. I think it is only right to point out that, in this case, as in other cases I have mentioned, the Government has absolutely disregarded, not only the interests, but the elementary rights of the greatest of our wealth-producing industries. It has set up from time to time that it has done these things in the interests of the prosecution of the war, but, in this case, if I may so, it has been caught with the goods. It commandeered wheat on the plea of urgency, and it has that wheat yet, and those on whose behalf it commandeered the wheat have not taken it away and have not furnished the transportation to take it away. Could there be anything with less excuse and less reason than the action which this

Government took; could there be less ground for blaming the war conditions or the needs of the Allies?

Might I be allowed to
make a comment or two upon some of the statements made by the hon. member for Edmonton? (Mr. Oliver). As a matter of fact we have absolutely no proof, beyond his assertion, as to the amount of grain which was held by the farmers. From the little knowledge I have of how' grain is handled in the western country, I say that there is a comparatively small amount of grain held by the farmers in the elevators at Fort William. Occasionally we meet a farmer of a speculative turn of mind who has become wealthy by growing grain in a large way, a man perhaps owning 50,000 acres, and he will handle his grain as an ordinary grain dealer. A few men of his kind may have had gram in the elevators at. Fort William, but the average farmer working a section, or a half-section or a quarter-section does not, as i rule, have very much gram m the elevators at Fort William, or anywhere else, except at home where he may have a little stored waiting for the price to rise to the point at which he can safely sell it. He will use the elevator in his home town to some considerable extent, but 1 have not known many cases where farmer would ship his grain to Fort William and hold it there. If the men engaged in the grain business have suffered as seriously as my hon. friend from Edmonton would suggest, the grain probably belonged to a man in the grain business and not to the farmer in the West. If a large quantity was held by the farmer, it would certainly mean no loss to the grain dealer, because he would have nothing to do with it; he would have advanced no money upon it* and would therefore have no claim upon that grain.
My hon. friend protested against the Government commandeering that grain and not taking it away immediately to the Atlantic coast. I ask, what difference would it make whether it was in the elevators at Fort William or down at the Atlantic coast, when it could not be shipped out of the country? What possible difference could it make to the grain dealer?
What earthly purpose was served 'by commandeering the grain if it was not possible to get it forward?

We will suppose that a gentleman in the Old Country wired an

order to a grain dealer at Fort William to buy him so much grain. The grain dealer secures that grain, and he sends it as far as Fort William and has it stored on the order of the man who has purchased it. He ha3 done his duty; he has complied with the terms of the order. It is then up to the man in the Old Country who has ordered that grain to get it away, to provide the accommodation across the Atlantic so as to allow the grain to go forward. If this Government, at the request of the people of the Old Country, secured so many million bushels of grain, I think they complied with the requirements of the case; they secured the grain. It may be a question, as the hon. gentleman indicates, whether they took the wisest course, or not. That is a question for debate.
Hear,'hear.

But I think they performed, their duty when they secured the grain, and1 we have -the positive assurance of the minister that it has gone forward as fast as it -could be removed from the Atlantic coast. What more could have -been done? I ask any reasonable man in this House, or in this country, Whether the Government has not done all it could do?
I do no,t think that the farmer in the West has suffered loss to the extent of a five-cent . piece, and I do not think the dealers have lost very much by the action of t'he Government. They might have lost if the Government had been in a position to take away the grain at once. They might have suffered some annoyance from delay in replacing the grain taken away. But when it was found that the grain could not be removed immediately they were allowed to take some of the grain and to replace it at Fort William at a later date- when it would suit the Government to have it removed to the Atlantic seaboard. Consequently, they -suffered no loss. In fact, I do not see how anybody suffered loss. I think the farmers of the West, as a class, got a better price- for their grain, following the action of the Government, than they would have got had the Government not taken that action, because the very fact that the Government stepped in and was storing grain had the effect of putting up the price. The price went up, and remained up for some considerable time as the result of the Government's action, and then it dropped back to the normal, and it has been lower ever since.
I understood my hon. friend to say that the action of the Government in commandeering the grain raised the price throughout the West?
Yes.
Then had the Government not better commandeer a little more and raise the price again?
If the hon. gentleman suggests that I have no objection at all.
Does my hon. friend make that suggestion?
If the Government can raise the price substantially on 100,000,000 bushels of grain by commandeering 10,000,000 bushels we all agree that they should do so.

The fact of the matter is that the price of grain went up, but when the grain could not be got out of the country the price began to fall. Compared with the price at Liverpool, I say that owing to the action of the Government the price was higher in the West than it was 'before, and than it is to-day.
Will the hon. gentleman not ^ urge the Government to heave it up again, to commandeer another 10,000,000 bushels ?
I leave that to the hon. gentleman, who seems to have the wellbeing of the farmers of the West at heart. Why does he not take action?
Because I do not think that the action of the Government had the effect which .my hon. friend says it had.

The hon. gentleman is quite entitled to his opinion, and I think I am entitled to mine, ^nd I think I know as much about the grain business as the hon. gentleman. I do not think that very much fault can be found with the Government for taking that action. I admit that it is a question open to debate, and every man is entitled to his opinion. In my opinion it was the wisest course to take in order to be sure of obtaining that much grain, because, if it had been left to be purchased in small quantities, as the hon. gentleman thinks it ought to have been, they might not have secured the grain as easily as they did. I do not see what good would have been accomplished by taking any other course and I do not see any point in the objection that
the hon. gentleman has raised. I think he is actuated more by a desire to find fault with the Government than by any other motive.
May I ask my hon. friend this? He considers that the action of the Government in commandeering the wheat raised the price and thereby conferred a benefit on the country-the farmer.
I did not say on the country; I said on the farmer.
On the farmer; but the reason given by the minister is that buying the grain in the ordinary course of business at that time would have raised the price.

I cannot say that I am surprised that the action taken by the Government in this case has met with the opposition of certain hon. members on the other side of the House. My experience of recent months has been that the more commendable the action the more violent and direct is the opposition. My imagination would fail me were I to try to conceive of any course this Government could fake that would not Joe described by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) as an attack upon the farmers of the West. If we commenced a system of distributing public money to each farmer individually, we would be met with a complaint by the hon. member that we were robbing the farmers of western Canada.
No harm in my hon. friend trying it.

But my hon. friend's argumentative attacks are often transparent fallacies. My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) takes the ground that the course adopted by the Government was an extraordinary one .and could only be justified by extraordinary causes. I do not know that I can take any exception to that' pronouncement. The leader of the Opposition, while by the accident of fate, he has passed through the world as a Liberal, is to those of us who know him best, anu I think to the country as a whole, well understood to be about the most pronounced Conservative, in the right mfeaniog of the term, that there is in Canada. If this Government does strike out upon new and strong lines in any matter, the first and the last to oppose is the leader of the Opposition. When we seek to ground our course on the plea of emergency, he is the loudest in disap-

proval, and sets to work to show, not always with success, that no such emergency exists. In the case of the appropriating of the wheat, the Government were faced with the necessity, as it appeared to them from the documents in hand, of procuring a large amount of wheat in a short time with the probaible necessity, through their agency or otherwise of procuring a larger quantity in a short time in the future. This appeared to us in definite form on the 23rd November. The courses open to us have been mapped out, and I do not need to relate them at length. But the Government could not go into the market, through an agent, and procure the wheat within the v time limited unless with results which we deemed would be inconsistent with our duties as agent and trustee. The Government, under the circumstances, selected men acquainted with the business whose advice would be valuable. The advice of these men was obtained, and not only under the circumstances were we able to obtain it as to the course to be pursued in respect to the actual purchasing of the grain, but as to the difficulties that would be met with in the purchasing of it by other means and as to the best method of solving those difficulties. The preponderance of view was that the proper course, consistently with our duty as the agent of the allied commission, and to the producers in Canada was to take the grain by appropriation. The views obtained wrere obtained in a confidential way as should be done in these cases. Two of the men whose views were so given have seen fit to state in part what they said to the Government and not to state the rest of it, but even with that I do not feel compelled to go farther and put the whole position assumed by these men, and assumed by the others who were called in, in reference to the matter, upon record. It may become necessary later on.

Is it true that one of
the largest and most reputable commission houses in Canada stated that they could get the grain without any extraordinary means?

It is quite true that
there was scarcely a commission house in Canada that was not ready to buy the grain at the usual rate of a cent a bushel. It would be a very strange commission house that would not be anxious to do that, but I am justified in saying this, in answer to my hon. friend from Moosejaw,

that there was not one who did not readily agree that for the Government to go into the market and get the grain that was required would result in the inflation of the market
Hear, hear.

The hon. member for
Edmonton says " hear, hear ". I know what he has in the back of his head-that had we gone about it by the means of sending of agents into the market the farmer would have received the benefit. No one denies that the farmer would have got the benefit just as he has it now. But there is one result which would have accrued, which has not by our method accrued, and that is that immense profits which would have gone to the middleman, who is usually the object of jealousy and attack on the part of the hon. member for Edmonton and other members of the Opposition, would have been extracted from the pockets of the Allies for whom' we were acting. The hon. gentleman does not say " hear, hear " to that, but he knows it.

Grain is handled for a
certain commission, a percentage of half a cent a bushel, and I suppose the buyers would have bought it on that commission.

No doubt they could
have bought it, and they would have been very glad to have done it. It will be observable to hon. members in this House that after villifying the middlemen, and all who look like middlemen, if it is necessary for the purpose of opposing the Government of the day, the hon. gentleman can quite readily assume the role of the champion of middlemen and agents. He says, and the leader of the Opposition backs him up in this assertion, that every purchaser is ready to pay a commission, and consequently the Government should be ready to let the commission man come in and get his commission on every purchase.

Would it not
have been possible, without employing any commission men at all, to have done exactly the same thing that you did in the purchase of seed grain-employ the men in your own department to purchase that grain, they getting their salaries and no commission?

That undoubtedly
would not have been possible. The only way to have got it otherwise would have been to have employed some one to get it

on the market and pay the usual commission.
You had Wesley Allison.

I have no doubt that
had these hon. gentlemen been in power ' that is just the course they would have pursued. I am going to the heart of this question; I am going to discuss it seriously, as it deserves.
And it needs discussion.

It needs discussion and it will get discussion. Hon. gentlemen say that we could have pursued the course of putting an agent, or agents, into the market and commissioning them at so much per bushel to buy the grain. It is argued that the amount procurable was not l^rge proportionately to the amount traded in at that time on the grain exchanges. In one sense that is true, but not in any sense that means anything in relation to this discussion. It is true that grain is traded in by the millions of bushels on the Grain Exchange. The same grain is traded in perhaps ten, perhaps fifty, perhaps a hundred times, and consequently the whole volume of trading is very great. The thirteen or fifteen million bushels, as in this case that we have in mind, might, before it ultimately reached a purchaser for export, have been traded in ten or a hundred times. But the purchase for actual export and use of thirteen or fifteen million bushels is a very large transaction, even in relation to the trading of the Grain Exchange. It may represent five, ten, or twenty times that amount of trading in volume as the grain in the usual way of trade proceeds. Now, I think I have made that clear.
There was not one of those who were called to give their opinion on the case, and who should have been qualified to give that opinion, who did not agree that it would have been utterly impossible to conceal the principal behind the agent, and to avoid, in part at all events, the result which accrued the year before-an inflation of the market to the benefit of the dealer and speculator in grain, and to the disadvantage of the consuming public and the Allied Commission. It was felt at the time that there would be some dislocation in regard to contracts already entered into, and means were canvassed by which that could be reduced to the minimum. The advice of those men was taken upon that and was followed, and I think they and the country are to be congratulated upon the thoroughness of
this work and the success which attended the reducing of that dislocation to a minimum. That, of course, appertained to the dealer alone, a man who is entitled to be treated fairly by Governments as by all, and that was the principal objection-'may I go further and say the only objection-urged against the course taken by the Government by those called in. No obejction against the course taken was offered by any one called in to advise the 'Government, and no objection, except for political reasons, could be urged to-day by any one except as it affected the middlemen, the dealers, and the speculators.

Who were the parties
whom the hon. member consulted?

Two of them the hon. gentleman knows; the others were eastern men. Personally I have no objection to giving the names; but, as the matter concerns the Department of Trade and Commerce, and as they wore called by the minister, I will leave him to decide whether or not he will give their names.

In all cases they were
dealers or speculators.

Oh, no. The hon.
gentleman seems to know who they were, but he wants to ask in order, if possible, that the names may be published.

We know perfectly well
that Mr. Crowe of the Winnipeg Grain Exchange and Mr. Crerar of the Grain Growers' Grain Association were consulted by the hon. gentleman, and they are dealers and middlemen.

Yes, and the objections were solely from that viewpoint; nor was it suggested by any one, nor would it be suggested to-day, except for purely political reasons, that from the point of view of the producer, the farmer, any possible objection could be taken.

Did the hon. member or
any of his friends consult the western farmers on the subject.

I- do not think that the association for which the hon. gentleman often stands up will stand beside him when he says that Mr. Crerar, of the Grain Growers' Grain Association, in no sense represents the western farmer. I am led to believe that he, in his position as representative of the Grain Growers' Grain Association, and his institution exist for the benefit of the western farmers.

And Mr. Crerar advised
against' this seizure.
Mr. ME1GHEN: Mr. Crerar did not advise against the seizure from the point of view of the farmer. So far as his advice and criticism went, they were based solely on the interference that would be caused to the trade in the hands of the middleman and the speculator. If 1 were to tell the hon. gentleman all that was said from the point of view of the farmer, I am sure it would be no comfort to his argument this afternoon. From the point of view of the farmer every consideration advanced was in favour of the commandeering.
It is only fair, when the hon. member brings authorities to bear upon the subject, that he should state what those authorities said.

I will be just as fair, and fairer, I think, than some of the speakers who have preceded me in this debate. The opinions of the gentlemen I do not intend to state, nor to give their names, further than they have given them themselves. The minister may do so if he desires.
Now we come to the actual results of the commandeering. To purchase in the open market, as to purchase by the method taken, would, as can be easily understood by any one acquainted with the trade, clearly bring about an increase in price; but as to which method would have the greater effect it was difficult to measure. Both methods would very likely bring about a rapid increase in price. To have adopted a method of purchasing in the open market within the time desired would immediately -all were agreed on this and all agree today-have resulted in something of the nature of an inflation in price. I ask hon. gentlemen opposite and also hon. members on this side: Would this Government, commissioned as a Government to act as- the trustee of the Allied Commission, have been justified in taking a course which would have added to the value not only of all the grain in the West, but of the grain sought to 'be purchased in store and brought about a largely inflated price for the benefit of those who held it in store and for the loss of those for whom the Government were acting?
Tt did not seem to bother the Government very much in the case of shells and fuses.

The hon. gentleman is anxious now to get on to the subject of shells and fuses. Some of his friends are just as anxious to get off the shells and fuses. Now we are discussing the question of wheat, and I intend to keep to it.

I think honestly the
hon. gentleman is sorry that he ever touched the wheat last fall.

The hon. gentleman
may decide what his opinions are; I presume he will give me the prerogative of deciding mine. I am discussing the effects of the course taken. The effects of the course we did not take would have been clear; it would have added at once very largely to the value of the grain in store to the benefit of the grain speculators. It is really refreshing to hear the hon. member say that some speculators told him that the loss to those men was $200,000, and that he thinks that we committed a great wrong. It seems to me that it is only about three weeks since the hon. member argued here that they were a band of ring-sters, a combine to extract money from the western farmers by depressing the price of wheat. Now he weeps tears be-, cause he finds the course we pursued took $200,000 from' their profits for the benefit of the Allied Commission. For myself, I do not think it did. They failed to make the money they otherwise would have made; there is no doubt about that, and they may regard that as a loss. They would have made the money if we had taken the course of -buying in the open market all the grain they held in store for speculation; and that may be how they measure their loss. If we had put commission merchants into the field to buy, every cent of rise in the price per bushel would have meant $130,000 out of the pockets of the Allied Commission and would not have meant a dollar in the pockets of the farmers of Canada beyond what by the rise actually took place. The course we pursued had the effect of raising the value of the wheat back of the elevators in Fort William in the hands of the farmers and unsold; it had-the effect of raising the level of markets all the way westward. The other course would have had that effect also; but this course did not have the effect of raising the value of the grain in the hands of the speculators and taking it out of the pockets of the Allied Commission, whereas the course my

hon. friend recommends would have done that.
What we were recommending was that they should leave trade to follow its own course when there was no urgency.

The course the hon. gentleman recommends would have put money into the pockets of the speculators of whom he is the champion this afternoon, and would have taken it out of the treasuries of the Allies, But the money that went to the owners of grain, by reason of the rise in value of the grain after the commandeering, went into the pockets of the farmers, and they have got it.
Could the hon. gentleman raise the price again?

When new cases arise . we will consider the circumstances and will be governed Iby the same considerations that governed us before, and I may tell the hon. gentleman that he has said nothing in this debate that will be considered worthy to enter into the discussion of that matter.
Seeing that the Allies have not got much of the wheat yet, it seems likely they will not deal with the Government again.

The hon. gentleman is complaining now on the part of the Allies. They got their grain at $1.04}, whereas his method, according to his own argument, would have given them the grain at $1.30, or something like that.
They have not got it at all.
They have got it so far as our delivery is concerned.

But they cannot eat your delivery.
. Mr. MEIGHEN: Had not the hon. gentleman better go across and help them? We have fulfilled our contract. Now, if the hon. gentleman has anything pertinent to the argument to interject I have no objection to be interrupted, but surely he does not think that he deceives me by complaining of the conduct of the Allies and attributing that to this Government. We took it for granted-and we have no reason yet to think we were misled-that the Allied Commission desiring the grain within a very limited time and would be able to take deliveries and get them over. No
doubt the Allied Commission believed they could^ do so; there is no question they had reason to believe they could. But the exigencies of war are beyond the exact measurement of even the Allied Commission, though possibly not beyond the exact measurement of the hon. member for Edmonton. The exigencies of war they were not able to take with accuracy into consideration and adjust their conduct exactly to them. Events arose, doubtless, which they had not in contemplation, and they were not able to get the grain across- which was their part of the work-within the time they had anticipated. But our end of the bargain was fulfilled, we lived up to our end of it by getting the grain for them and getting it at a fair price, the market price. That was the fulfilment of our duty to the Allies for whom we were acting.

How much did the Allies ask should be secured for them?
Mr .MEIGHEN: Hon. gentlemen have asked that ad infinitum, and they have been told it, so far as we can tell it, by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. The ordeT that was given us was filled. There [DOT]were other messages and negotiations preceding the order which affected the necessities of the order as actually given, and which made it our plain duty to have that order filled within a very limited time, and, to that end, to get the grain by the expropriation method. Any other method would have inflicted upon those fox whom we were acting a severe toss from which the farmers themselves would have gained no benefit beyond what they have gained by the method adopted.

I desire to correct the statement of the hon. minister. I did not ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce before what the quantity was. I did ask as to the time. Of course, if the minister does not care to tell the amount, that is all right.
The question was asked and answered, and I thought it was the hon. member from Moosejaw who asked it.
I was not here when the question was answered, and perhaps the hon. gentleman will tell me what the answer was.
The amount is represented by the amount delivered.
But how much did they ask the Government to secure?

The figures are on
record-some 13,000,000 bushels were actually commandeered.

Did the Allies ask for
13,000,000 bushels or what more did they ask for?

The amount they got
represented what they asked for.

The hon. gentleman
does not need to answer if he does not wish to do so.
Has the hon. gentleman understood that it was 13,000,000 bushels?
Did they ask for 13,000,000 bushels?

I do not recall the exact wording of it, but it was put within such limits that the amount we actually procured for them in this way fulfilled the order. The hon. gentleman knows that it is not possible to place on record the communications that passed in regard to that matter between tbi3 Government and the Allies; if not he has not any adequate sense of his responsibilities ae a member of Parliament. These communications, as one can well understand, contain statements of fact and apprehensions which should not be made public, and no man with a proper sense of durty would ask that they should be made public.

Surely you can make
that much public.

That much has been
made public.
When?

In the House-now.
How often does the hon. gentleman want an answer? The order was given in such terms that the grain procured at the time amounted to a fulfilment of the order as to the grain required and as to the time. I do not see that any more is pertinent to the case. It is argued that there was a dislocation of trade, and a peculiar twist of reasoning was gone through by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) that all the grain except that received from the farmers we gave back-that the farmers had three million bushels and the dealers and millers had seven and a half million bushels, and that we gave back the grain to the others, and we kept that of the farmers and have it yet. The grain we gave back 
was returned within ten days, or rather it was not given back at all but merely loaned in order that there might be no stoppage in the fulfilment of orders and the outflow of grain at Fort William. It was all done under contract, duly secured, for the return of the grain in the same channel, and it was returned-and that is all there is to this assertion about delay. And not only that, but by the centralization and control exercised at Fort William by the adoption of that method, greater speed was made than ever was known before in the history of that port. The hon. gentleman has complained of a delay of a day or two. There was no delay; there was no cause for delay. I know that the order was given on Saturday night and the following morning, on request from Fort William, I myself instructed them, on behalf of the Government, that there should be no delay whatever in the loading of any vessel or in the pouring out of the grain through the funnel at Fort William.
Was this the only order received from that commission?

No, other orders have
been received at various times, perhaps not from this special commission.

How were they dealt
with?

I do not recall whether it was in pursuance of a foreign order or not, but we did on a former occasion commandeer another class of grain. Other orders have been filled by purchase, but in those cases there, was time enough to make purchases without unduly affecting the market and without loss to those for whom we were acting.
I was dealing with the question of delay. By means of the organization and centralization of control in the department, so far from there being any delay in the pouring through of the grain, there was expedition, there was facilitation, there was a saving of time. Within a period of four or five days after the commandeering of the grain, there was a larger issuance of grain from Fort William than ever before in the history of the port. Let me give, as it were, a picture of the method followed. Fort William is like a great funnel through which the western grain pours. After the commandeering, the grain continued to pour through that funnel as before but expedited by the fact that the Grain Commission controlled the vessels into which the grain went, and were able to see to it that each

vessel was loaded fully at one elevator, instead of passing from elevator to elevator. The grain continued to pour through that funnel with greater expedition than it had come through before. But while it was doing so such grain as was necessary to fill orders went to the fulfillment of those orders, and the remainder of the grain as it entered the funnel was appropriated to the purposes of the Government order. That is a picture of what actually took place. There was virtually no dislocation in that regard. There was great fear of dislocation. There was, indeed, very great apprehension, particularly on the part of grain dealers in Winnipeg, that it would not be possible to' meet these difficulties in any adequate way, and that these dealers stood to suffer great losis. But when they were apprised of the actual method adopted to adjust the situation and to meet all their legitimate demands, they were one and all loud in their approval of it. I wish to endorse what the Minister of Trade and Commerce says in regard to these men. It was our desire to keep down their losses, to keep down even their apprehension, to the lowest possible point. It was their desire, I believe, to meet us in every way that they could, even if they felt that it would be at a loss to themselves. They did meet us in a proper spirit; they assisted the Government by every means in their power in the carrying out of the appropriation in such manner as to .result in the least possible disoomiforture and inconvenience. I believe also that the farmers of the West, except, possibly, a few who may be of the same mind as hon. gentlemen opposite, or too much under their influence, have approved the course adopted.
I would like to ask the minister if he has any information as to how much of the grain in the elevators belonged to the farmers?

I cannot give the exact figures, but I am glad the hon. gentleman mentioned that. Very careful inquiries were made before the appropriation took place as to .about what percentage would be unsold in the 'hands1 of the farmers. The figure that was generally adopted -indeed, I think it was the only percentage that was suggested-was twenty-five per cent. I think the Estimates given were all about the same; it has worked out something like that. There have been complaints that grain that really had not been appropriated at all was paid
203	.
for by grain' companies at the commandeered price, on the representation that, the grain was included in the appropriated grain. It may be-indeed I think it is a fact-that grain that was never really appropriated and that still remained the property of the farmer was represented- perhaps* innocently in some cases-by grain dealers as being appropriated and was settled for by the grain dealer with the farmer at the appropriated price. We have had complaints along that line. In fact, the Grain Commission, whose duty it has been to follow up such cases wherever complaint was made, have compelled grain merchants in many cases actually to pay to the farmer the additional price because they had settled on the representation that the grain had been appropriated, although it had not been appropriated at all. The final outcome of At all is this: about 3,000,000 odd bushels of farmers' grain and about 10,000,000 odd bushels of speculators' grain were appropriated at Fort William. All of it was paid for at the market price. Previous to the date of appropriation the market had been a slightly rising one. Whether it would have continued to rise an hour longer, no human 'being could say. It might have fallen the very next day; we cannot tell-it might have risen. At all events, previous to the appropriation the price had been rising, and $1.04} was paid for No. 1 Northern wheat. One would almost think, to hear hon. gentlemen opposite argue, that to appropriate grain was to commit some awful injustice; that to buy grain or anything else at the market price was doing the owner or proprietor of the grain very serious injury. There is ho doubt the fact that unless circumstances otherwise demand it is the right of an individual to choose his own time of selling, but to say that serious injury or any injury is done is to exaggerate the facts. I have heard it argued by hon. gentlemen opposite-I think by the hon. member for Edmonton-why do you not expropriate the manufacturer's product? You expropriate the product of the farmer; why not expropriate that of the manufacturer? Well, there are some manufacturers in this House and I put to them the question whether one of them would not be very glad if the Government came along and expropriated all his product at the market price? Would there be a happier day for him in the whole history of his manufacturing career?
Not if on a rising market.

If on a rising market, neither he nor any one else knows whether the market will rise for another hour. If he does know it, he is, able to go on the market and buy against his belief and make money on the rise. However, I do^not say that it wo.uld be the part of any farmer to go and buy against it. He got the full value of the grain that he had in store the day that it was appropriated, and he got more than that: he got the added value to every bushel that he had behind, and I do not think there were many farmers in western Canada of those who had grain in store who did not have several bushels behind for every one that they had in store. He got the profit that accrued by reason of the increment of value added to what he had left, and he got a fair price for every bushel that he sold. So that, taking it all in all, the farming community of Canada, by virtue of the course taken, were the gainers not by thousands, but by hundreds of thousands-yes, by millions. They would have been gainers also had we taken the other course. The speculators were not by our method losers. On the other hand, they were not the gainers that they would have been if we had taken the course suggested toy hon. gentlemen opposite. They were not the gainers at the expense of our principals, the Allied Commission in Europe. That is what I conceive to be good Government business; that is the course a good Government should pursue. Where it can eliminate the middleman it should do so; where it can act for the benefit of its principals, it should, as any other agent do so faithfully and firmly. That is what we did in this case; we did it to the advantage of the producers and to the advantage of our principals, and they are the parties whose interests we were bound to have in mind.

Ever
since the House assembled in January last we have been waiting with a good deal of curiosity to know what reasons would be given by my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce for the unusual course that was taken by the Government in commandeering the wheat required for the Allied countries. We certainly expected that there would be some good reason behind the action that would justify the Government in dislocating the trade of the country to the extent which it did, but when my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and his colleague the Solicitor General, the two ministers who were interested in carrying the transaction through, gave their explanation before the Committee to-day we found that they had really no excuse to give other than that in their judgment the course which they took was the best in the circumstances. My hon. friend the Solicitor General, complained that there was nothing that the Government could do that would satisfy the Oppositicm. I am prepared to agree with the hon. gentleman that we cannot expect much from this Government that we on this side of the House would be able to agree with. One reason that was given by the Won. the Solicitor Genera], and one which he seemed to think would cover up everything else, was that, by commandeering 13,000,000 bushels of wheat last November, the Government raised the price of wheat to the farmer in the West. Let us look into this for a few moments to see what justification, if any, there is for that statement on the part of the Solicitor General. At the time that the wheat was commandeered, there were at least 200,000,000 bushels of wheat in the '* West to be sold.
My hon. friend suggests that the action of the Government in taking 13,000,000, out of 200,000,000 bushels, had the effect of raising the price of wheat and making every bushel that the farmer had worth more than it was before. You might as well say that if a dozen farmers brought in 200 bushels of potatoes to sell on the Ottawa

market, and one householder in Ottawa bought thirteen bushels, that would put the price of potatoes up all over Canada, because the percentage would be the same. That is only one of the absurdities of the argument of hon. gentlemen opposite. You must remember that the price of wheat went up all over the United States at the same time. As a matter of fact, our Canadian market simply followed the trend of the market of the United States. For many days prior to the 27th November, when the minister commandeered this wheat, the price had been advancing, and surely no man in his senses would say that, because my hon. friend took 13,000,000 'bushels off the market .by commandeering it, or in any other way, he had put up the price on the
200.000.	000 bushels in Canada and on the
700.000.	000 or 800,000,000 bushels in the United States. The 13,000,000 would be about one per cent of the wheat that was affected. And our hon. friends offer that to the farmers of the West as an excuse for the action the Government took in commandeering this wheat, and try to get out of an awkward corner by attempting to make the farmer believe that the action they took has given him a better price. It is not possible to tell absolutely what my hon, friend had in his mind when he did this. I would be inclined to believe that the minister did w.hat he thought was the viery best under the circumstances. I am inclined to believe, also, that his colleague, the Solicitor General, thought he was going to pull off a good political stunt. At that time there was a good deal of agitation for free wheat, provided I may be allowed by the Minister of Trade and Commerce to mention free wheat again in this House this session. There was considerable agitation at that time for free wheat, and the Solicitor General took this view of the matter: Now, here is an opportunity to commander 13,000,000 bushels of wheat. Usually just 'as navigation is closing for the season there is a drop in the price of wheat. Of course, my hon. friend had to take soma chancels, because for a considerable time the price of wheat had been going up; but as soon as navigation closes the price usually drops down. The Solicitor General, I imagine, expected to find himself in the position that the Government had commandeered a certain amount of wheat, a large percentage of which was owned by the farmers in the West, and as these particular farmers would have received an enhanced price for their wheat,
203*
it would have shown the acuteness of the Government and that the Government were working in the farmers' interests. Unfortunately for the calculations of my hon. friend, if that was his view, the very opposite took place. The commandeering of this wheat, instead of enabling my hon. friend to make political capital, has 'acted as a boomerang. The price of wheat kept going up, and the farmers who had wheat stored at that time, and who had to take the price that was offered with no option in the matter, are the men who have suffered and are complaining bitterly about the way they have been treated.
The minister said to-day that it was perfectly right that the farmer, generally speaking, should be allowed to decide his own time and to use his own judgment as to when he would sell his wheat and what price he would take for it. No one is complaining that the price received for that wheat was not a fair price. It is a pretty fair price-$1,041 at Fort William for No. 1 Northern. But surely the farmer had the right to say whether he would sell that wheat at that price or not. If my hon. friend had offered to buy that wheat from the farmers, very many of them would have sold probably at that price. But there were hundreds of farmers who had wheat down there, and who did not want to sell at that time. These were men who had got their threshing done, had sold a car or two of wheat to settle up the .accounts connected with the threshing, the store accounts, and the account for growing the crop. They expected that the price of wheat would go up, and they had shipped their wheat down to Fort William intending to hold it for the spring market. You must remember that a farmer cannot hold wheat in his home elevator. No country elevator, whose business is to handle wheat, not to store wheat for a long time, will allow itself to be filled up by holding the wheat there. A farmer puts wheat in the elevator on the understanding that the elevator has the right to ship that wheat down to the head of the lakes and put it in storage there. It does not make any difference to the farmer; it does not cost him any more to store it at Fort William than it does at the home point. He is quite agreeable to that, and if he wants to hold the wheat until the following spring, or to take advantage of any advance in price during the winter, he puts his wheat in storage at Fort William or Port Arthur. If he desires to sell all he has to do is to sign his certificate, hand it over to the

buyer, and get his cheque for the amount. I want to assure the Solicitor General and the minister that there was a great deal of that wheat /held by the farmers. It was acknowledged .to-day in the House that there was something like 25 per cent owned by farmers. My information is, and I got it from a prominent member of the Grain Exchange who was in a good position to know-and if I am astray in my figures, the minister, who probably knows exactly, can set me right-that there were over
5,000,000 bushels of this wheat belonging to farmers stored there and not sold on that day. Those farmers have lost quite a sum of money. A number of farmers in my constituency have brought the matter to my, attention. One of them whom I ran across down here a month or so ago told me that he had three cars of wheat at Fort William, the wheat was commandeered, and at the time he was speaking to me the loss was about $750. Another farmer in the vicinity of Frobisher had 10,000 bushels of wheat in store at Fort William that he was holding for spring, and at the time he wrote to me about it he could have sold for $1.25 a bushel, whereas the price he got from my hon. friend was $1,041, so that he was out $2,500 on the transaction. There are scores and hundreds of farmers throughout the prairie country who have suffered just in the way that the two I have instanced have suffered. I imagine that none of those farmers would object to having his wheat commandeered if it had been a necessity in connection with the war, a necessity for Great Britain or for Canada, or even for any of the Allies of Great Britain; but the position they take, and naturally so, is that this was done without any justification; that the minister could have procured his 13,000,000 bushels of wheat without causing a ripple on the wheat market and without dislocating or disrupting the trade or causing any inconvenience for anybody connected with the trade.
One of the ministers stated this afternoon that the Government had taken advice on this matter. We do not know all to whom they applied for advice, but we know that Mr. Crowe, one of the most prominent grain buyers in Winnipeg, and Mr. Crerar, President of the Grain Growers' Grain Association in Winnipeg, advised against the course which the Government took; at least, they said so in interviews which were published in the newspapers and which I have never seen contradicted. Mr. Rich-

ardson, of Kingston, probably the largest grain dealer in Canada, stated that his advice was absolutely against it, and that grain could have been purchased without interfering in any way with the trade, without hurting anybody, and without raising the price. Mr. Richardson instanced one occasion on which there was only 4,000,000 bushels of Kansas red spring wheat on the market, of which his firm had purchased
2,500,000	bushels without raising the price a fraction of a cent. At the very time that my hon. friend commandeered this wheat, wheat was pouring into Fort William at the rate of two or three million bushels a day; so that the question was only one of a week's receipts, and, by giving a broker an order to buy it quietly, the wheat could have been purchased without causing any disturbance whatever.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce stated that you could not buy from the farmers. I do not think tljat is correct. On the very day that my hon. friend commandeered that wheat, there were millions and tens of millions of bushels of wheat throughout the West, every elevator where the grain had been threshed being practically filled to its capacity at the end of November. As I pointed out the other day, my hon. friend could have bought that wheat, because the market price for wheat in the elevators of the West was practically ten cents a bushel less than the market price for wheat on the track ready to be taken to Fort William, for which the price of $1.04 was paid. It would have been a boon to the country to have taken that wheat out of the elevators in the West, and it could have been taken out by the National Transcontinental and been landed at Portland or at St. John, provided that the Government had given the same rate over the whole route as over the part from Armstrong to Quebec, and in that way they would have procured the wheat at a lower price for their customers, the Allied Governments. Yet my hon. friend or his colleague this afternoon laid great stress on the duty of the Government to buy this wheat at the best possible price, I think, for the Kingdom of Italy. In that case, why did they buy November wheat on the 27th of November? Why did they not buy December options? At that time December wheat was six or seven cents a bushel less than November wheat; and, as the minister apparently knew that they did not need the wheat then, he could just as well have bought the wheat to be

delivered a little later, and secured it at about seven cents a bushel cheaper, if he was working so hard in the interest of Italy, which was to get the bulk of the wheat. To prove that my hon. friend did not need the wheat then, I may say that no sooner had he commandeered the wheat than there was such a rumpus raised by the dealers and the millers that he immediately, out of the 13,000,000 bushels, turned back 7,500,000 bushels to be replaced later on. Therefore he could just as well have bought December wheat and paid that much less for the people for whom he was purchasing.
Another statement made this afternoon was that there was the utmost need of haste to meet the dire necessities of Italy, who, previous to going into this war, had sold herself short of wheat, and therefore had to get a great deal more, and that as a consequence the Government could not wait an hour, but must immediately commandeer the wheat. That sounds very well, but it does not bear analysis. At the ordinary rate of consumption of wheat by people who use wheat flour, the people of Italy from November 27 to the present time would have consumed about 120,000,000 bushels of wheat. That is taken on the basis of seven bushels per head of the population, which would be a fair average for a country of English-speaking people. Italy, however, may not use so much wheat; she may use more of other kinds of grain or of fruit. Let us suppose that she uses only two-thirds as much wheat as Englishspeaking nations, that would still leave about 80,000,000 bushels that she has consumed from November 27 to the present time. If there had been the necessity for haste which one would judge there was from the way in which this Government undertook to procure the wheat, Italy would many months ago have had at the various ports sufficient tonnage to take 15,000,000 bushels of wheat across the ocean. Therefore the argument that tremendous haste was necessary does not hold good for a minute. As my hon. friend from Edmonton pointed out this afternoon, this wheat was no sooner secured than the Government undertook to satisfy the millers and the dealers. The large millers were given all the wheat they needed, and the dealers were given wheat to fulfil their contracts, but no farmer was given the option of taking his wheat back and making other disposition of it. The farmers were left
out of the deal. There were, however, a good many small millers who suffered very much from this high-handed manner of dealing with the wheat.
Take the case of the small miller in the East who had made contracts for 10,000 or 20,000 bushels of wheat. That wheat is in the elevator at Fort William awaiting shipment. The commandeering takes place. These mills have no contract for the delivery of flour to any of the allied countries, therefore they do not come under the rule which would allow them to borrow their wheat back from the Government. But these mills have contracts with buyers, bakers and flour dealers all over the country. When they bought wheat they sold flour to a similar amount-that is the practice with the miller. So, in this case, the miller had bought his wheat and, on the basis of the price he paid, had sold his flour. The Government steps in and takes his wheat, and he has to go on a rising market and buy at an advance of five or ten cents a bushel, and yet he must sell his flour at the price at which he contracted to sell it. In this way many small mills through the country have lost large sums. The men who got out all right are the big millers and the big dealers- which is what usually happens in the transactions made by hon. gentlemen opposite; the smaller dealers, and the farmers particularly, get no consideration whatever, nor have they power to help themselves in such a case as this. Did I understand the Minister of Trade and Commerce to say that when the allied Governments ordered' wheat they ordered oats also?
No.

Probably I got that confused with the statement he made that oats had been commandeered once before. There is one point I would like cleared up. Would the minister say just what part of this 13,000,000 bushels of wheat was shipped out of Fort William before the close of navigation?
I have not the exact figures before me, -but I think it must have been about 7,000,000 bushels.
Then, do I understand that the rest of the wheat is still at Fort William?
That would not necessarily follow.

Was there a special rate on it by rail? Perhaps the minister would

say whether there was a rate on it of six cents a bushel from Fort William to Quebec.
I do not think there was any rate of that kind.

I found it a little difficult to harmonize' the statement that approximately three-quarters of the wheat commandeered had already been shipped to the allied countries with the other statement that only about one-half had been shipped out of Fort William before the close of navigation-unless, of course, it was sent down at the high Canadian Pacific rate by land during the winter months. At all events the 'Government has apparently had enough of commandeering wheat, and the allied countries have apparently had enough of ordering wheat through the Government; both are apparently satisfied to leave each other alone for the future. The minister stated this afternoon that these foreign countries were still buying wheat in Canada; but, as I understand, they have not ordered any more wheat through the Government. I think that in that they show wisdom. Evidently the whole transaction did not prove very attractive to them, even though the Government was not charging any commission -of which a strong point was made this afternoon. Apparently these allied governments are satisfied that when they want wheat it is better to go to an ordinary dealer and buy it in the ordinary way. I am very glad these governments have come to that conclusion, because, in spite of the argument of the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) and the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. Wright), I am satisfied that the commandeering of the wheat did not raise the price of wheat by a fraction of a cent, and so did not benefit the farmers. On the other hand, the farmers who had not sold their wheat, but had it in storage, lost, probably, half a million dollars on the wheat they had.

During this afternoon something was said -I want to bring this to the attention of the Minister-about an investigation being made by the Grain Commission into cases where dealers had settled with farmers on the basis that their wheat, stored at Fort William and Port Arthur, had been commandeered, whereas it really had not been commandeered at all. I wish
to make a few remarks on some of the questions raised by the Minister of Trade and Commerce this afternoon, not so much with regard to the commandeering of the wheat as with regard to the policy that has been pursued by this Government since 1911 oin the question of terminal -elevators. The minister apparently takes a great deal of credit to himself and to the Government for the establishment of the Grain Commission and the general policy 9 p.m. that has been followed since the establishment of that commission with regard to terminal elevators in Canada. The minister is no doubt aware that the Grain Act which he introduced dn the beginning of the year 1912 was exactly the- same Grain Act, with one or two exceptions, the chief of which I shall mention in a moment, as that which had been introduced into the Canadian Senate during the reciprocity session of 1911, but which never got as far as the House of Commons. However, the grain men and representatives of farmers' organizations in the various provinces of the West appeared before the Banking and Commerce Committee of the -Senate and a general agreement was arrived at as to what the Grain Act should be. In 1912, after the present Government assumed office,- the minister introduced a Bill, which so far as the Grain Commission and the principle of Government control is concerned, was exactly the
same act as that which had been practically passed by the Canadian Senate under Liberal administration in the year 1911. Whatever success, therefore, has come from the Grain Act as at present existing and the system of Government control may largely be attributed to the fact that under Liberal administration there were men who knew something about the situation and were able to cope with it. I must say that I believe that the system of Government control in connection with the grain situation in Canada has proved fairly successful. In the sessions of 1909, 1910, and 1911 the question of Government control and Government ownership and operation of terminal elevators was discussed in this House. On two different occasions members of the then Opposition from western Canada moved resolutions in the House of Commons in favour of Government ownership and operation of terminal elevators. The last resolution, moved in tile w-nter of 1911, was to the effect that the Government should acquire by lease, expropriation or otherwise-these were the very words used in 'the resolution-the terminal elevators of Canada. The question before the House of Commons on that occasion was not the establishment of one Government elevator, but the acquiring by lease, expropriation or otherwise of elevators throughout the country. That was the policy of the men who now occupy the treasury benches. In the sessions of 1909, 1910 and 1911 the policy advocated by members of the present Opposition, then supporters of the Government, was the policy of Government control that was carried out in their Grain Act of 1911 and adopted by this Government when it came into power.	I remember hearing the
present Prime Minister in the city of Regina in the month of July, 1911, during the recess in the reciprocity session of this Parliament.	In the western newspapers
he was reported as expressing himself in exactly the' same way as he expressed himself on the platform in the city of Regina. He said on that occasion that if the Conservative party were returned to power, if he were leading the Government of this country, the Government would take over the terminal elevators throughout Canada. How has this Government fulfilled that pledge? I am not saying that I was in favour of that policy. I was always in favour and am now in favour of a system of Government control of terminal elevators. But the members of the present
