Government, then in opposition, promised the people, on public platforms as well as on the floor of Parliament, that they would take over, own and operate the terminal elevators of this country. I believe the people of this country expect that an) political party that is elected to administer the affairs of Canada is bound to carry out in some degree at least the pledges that its supporters make to the people while they are carrying on an election campaign, particularly those planke of their platform that they vote for in the House of Commons. I venture to say that the present Minister of Trade and Commerce voted for Government ownership and operation of terminal elevators in the House of Commons on more than one occasion. If he did not it was because he was not present, because every other member of his party did and the members of western Canada particularly from Manitoba, were one and all in favour of Government ownership and operation of terminal elevators. In so far as the carrying out of that policy is concerned all the Government did was to establish one terminal elevator at Fort William. It is true that they established an elevator at Vancouver and interior elevators in Saskatchewan and Alberta, but, so far as any effect on the grain trade or on the general grain situation is concerned, all this Government has done is to establish one Government terminal elevator at Fort William. They might just as well have allowed a private company to build that elevator for all the effect it has had on the grain trade. That was done as a sop to the people of western Canada, in order to show that the Government were going to fulfil their pledges. Take the interior elevators established in Alberta and Saskatchewan-at Saskatoon, Moosejaw, and Calgary. I never heard any demands from the people of western Canada for the establishment of those elevators. Certain it is that the Grain Growers' organization of Saskatchewan or the United Farmers of Alberta never asked for the establishment of any interior storage elevators. Experience has proved during the last two years that except when there was an exceedingly big crop, and when the railways took the position they did this year by placing an embargo on the shipment of grain east of certain points, the interior elevators are of little use, because the people will not use them. In the Calgary elevator, in January, there was something over 200,000 bushels.

In Moosejaw a very small percentage of the space was filled at that time and the same situation existed in Saskatoon, although to a lesser degree, because there was a little more grain in that elevator in January and February than in the other two. But the people will not use these elevators unless they are forced to do so. They were forced to do so this winter on account of the exceedingly large crop, and on account of the fact that the railways could not haul out the grain because they would not accept shipments for eastern points. But I venture the opinion that in an ordinary year the interior elevators, would be of very little, if any, use. Take the terminal elevator at the city of Vancouver. I wonder if the minister imagines that that elevator is of any use at the - present time. I have not information as to how much grain there is in it at present, but only a very small percentage of the space was filled in January and February of this year, according to the information I have. I am informed by men who know traffic conditions of the Pacific that there will have to be an entirely new class of boat constructed for Pacific traffic through the Panama canal before you can handle any grain through the Vancouver elevator. I am informed that no boats of the type that carry grain on the Atlantic now exist on the Pacific. If that is the case I do not believe, and I do not believe that the minister believes, that the Vancouver elevator will be of any practical use for the next ten or fifteen years. I s>ay it was built simply on the system that goes in this country, the system of party patronage, which the minister so eloquently condemned in this House a short time ago, and I agree with everything he said on that occasion. The only reason for the construction of the Pacific coast elevator was the demand of the Conservative party in Vancouver. That is the opinion generally expressed throughout the West. We have had an absolute about-face on the part of the Government on this question since the days when they were in opposition.. All the western 'Conservative members, especially those from Manitoba, have simply turned their coats on this question ~of terminal elevators. They were, one and all, in favour of the Government operation of terminal elevators, just as we used to hear the Solicitor General championing the rights of the western farmer with respect to a lower tariff in this county-yet at every oppor-

tunity since this Government came into power the tariff has been increased, and the Solicitor General has on each occasion been one of the first to champion the increase. Instead of being the champion of the western farmer now, he has lost sympathy with the western people in general, because not only the western farmer but the western resident in general is interested in these matters. The Solicitor General and other Conservative members of Parliament from western Canada in this House, since they came into power and got near the treasury benches, have simply turned their coats on this question which so largely affects the people of the West.
The commandeering of wheat has been so ably discussed by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) and the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) that I hesitate to take up the time of the House, and particularly of the Government, by dealing with it at further length. I agree with what was stated by the hon. member for Assiniboia about the present situation in Parliament. I have been trying to find out what we have been here for since the Easter holidays.
Hear, hear.

I am glad that the Minister of Trade and Commerce agrees. If he would get his, colleagues together and get them to agree to some kind of railway legislation, so that we could have it before us and know what we were doing,' we might be out of here in two or three days. As it is we may be here for two or three weeks. There was no reason for our coming back here after the Easter holidays. The Minister of Trade and Commerce or any other member on that side of the House may attempt, if he likes, to blame the Opposition for the present condition of affairs. I say that the Government of this country is responsible for what goes on in this House. We are waiting to-day for a line of Government policy in regard to the railway situation, a very serious situation, but we have heard nothing of such a policy. Is it possible that the Government cannot agree on this question and place something before the House which we may consider and then get back to our homes, where we ought to be.
In regard to the commandeering of wheat, if the Minister of Trade and Commerce, as he has stated to-day, was convinced that there was an urgent need- apd no doubt there was an urgent needfor this grain among some of the allied nations, particularly Italy. If the people of Italy were in dire need at that time, they must be either starving or starved to-day, if they are still waiting for the Canadian grain. It appears to me that before the wheat was commandeered in this country, two conditions should have existed. One, I think, existed according to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, that was the condition' of dire need. The other circumstance that should have existed was transportation facilities for the carriage of the grain. Otherwise there was no reason for adopting such a high-handed method to get a sufficient quantity of grain to satisfy the Allies. Why did not the Minister of Trade and Commerce or the Government find out if these means of transportation existed ? The hon. Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) says it was the business of the British Government and the allied powers to see that the boats were there; that it was none of our business; that all we had to do was to grab so much wheat and say: Now it is there, come and get it. I say that before the Government took such highhanded action and went aside from the ordinary channels of business, they should have satisfied themselves first of the condition of dire need, and secondly, that the means of transportation were available to take the grain for the Allies' Commission. The second condition certainly did not exist and yet the Government commandeered some 13,000,000 bushels of wheat. That, to my mind, is the case in a nutshell. And what is the condition of affairs to-day? According to what has been stated by the minister to-night, some 7,000,000 bushels of the commandeered grain has actually gone across the Atlantic. The other 6,000,000 or
7,000,000 bushels is still in some elevators in Canada. The minister says it does not follow that because it has not all gone out of the country it is still at Fort William. It may be that the men who>
borrowed the grain have not yet seen fit to fulfil their obligations and return it to the Government, as the minister said, in ten days. I have not heard the minister say that that is the case; I am only suggesting that possibly they have not returned the grain which they borrowed from the Government. In so far as	this question relates
to the price of wheat, nobody in this House, nobody in this country, believes for one minute that the commandeering or purchasing of 13,000,000 bushels of grain in a market of 300,000,000 bushels

had any effect whatever on the price. I suppose that if the price had gone down, the Government would have said to the farmers in the West: Your wheat was needed and you have got an increased price anyway. But the commandeering had no effect on the market. The price did go up, hut not half as much as it did a year ago. The Government says it increased the price of wheat. No person imagines that the purchase of a very small quantity of the total Wheat crop of western Canada would have a cent's worth effect on the price of the whole production. The Solicitor General says that before they decided to commandeer the wheat they consulted a good many grain men, but the hon. member for Assiniboia has pointed out that three of those men, who apparently were consulted, have stated that they advised against it. I presume that they advised that the grain might be procured by the ordinary methods of business, by having somebody purchase it. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said that there were three ways by which the grain might have been procured. First, it might have been purchased directly from the farmer; secondly, it might have been procured through a	broker, and,	thirdly, it	mightbe	commandeered. I think	then
is another method by which it might have been secured, namely, by making use of the Grain Commission, which is a very efficient body, or through some person associated with the Grain Commission. If I am not seriously mistaken the Grain Commission with its .staff of officers could have procured thait grain without the payment of one cent to a middleman. That would of course have satisfied the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen). When I listened to the discussion this afternoon, it seemed to me that there was a great difference between the method adopted by the Government, and the reasons given for its adoption, and the method adopted in the purchase of seed grain for the farmers in the West during the season of 1915. To-day, the Government says it was very anxious to save commission to the middleman. It is all anxiety on behalf of the .prospective purchaser. i It was not the Minister of Trade and Commerce who purchased the seed grain; if he had had to do with it I am confident that it would have been handled in a much more efficient and economical manner than it was. I contend that it was done in a most wasteful manner. In 
1915 it was the vendor of the seed grain that the Government was anxious about, the man from whom the Government would select 200 or 300 bushels out of perhaps
3,000	bushels. That was the man about whom the Government was anxious, the vendor of the grain, and not the prospective purchaser, who, in the spring of 1915, had to pay $1.50 for his seed grain. In the session of 1915, after I had investigated the grain market prices during the months of January, February, and March, 1915, and of November and December, 1914-1 got the prices from Fort William, and the average price paid by the Government in each one of those months for the seed of the western farmer-and I proved that the average price paid by the Government in each of those months was higher than the ordinary price at Fort William, after making allowance for transportation charges, by from ten cents to twenty^six cents per bushel. It was not the prospective purchaser then whom the Government was anxious about, but, as I have said, the vendor. I am very glad that the Minister of Trade and Commerce did not employ the same officials, or the same class of men, to purchase the grain commandeered for the allied countries as were employed in purchasing the seed grain for the western farmers in 1915.

I want to deal with a matter concerning the province of Alberta, particularly the southern part of that province. Tt is in regard to the location of the internal storage elevator at the city of Calgary. I happened to deal with this matter when 1 spoke on the Budget, but the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce was not in the House at the time, and I would like to repeat some of the observations I made then. My contention is that the location of the elevator at Calgary was absolutely unwarranted. The explanation offered by the minister, in reply to a question I asked earlier in the session, was that the Calgary elevator was not intended to be, and is not, favourably situated for shipping grain east to Fort William. There is no question that it is not favourably situated for shipping grain east to Fort William. I maintain that the expenditure of money on an elevator in the province of Alberta could have been made to serve both western and eastern shipments of grain if the elevator had been located further south, on the Crow's Nest branch of the Canadian Pacific rail-

way, and I will try to offer to the minister what I think are substantial grounds for that argument. Calgary, as the minister knows, is practically on the ' border of the wheat-raising area of the province of Alberta. From Calgary north, the farming is practically of a [DOT] mixed character. From Calgary west it is ranching, and from Calgary east there is a considerable amount of grain grown. In the southern part of Alberta there is a great proportion of the wheat-raising section of the province. Any farmer east of Calgary shipping to the head of the lakes, and desiring to use an internal storage elevator would, if shipping by the main line, use the elevator at Moosejaw. If a farmer shipped along the Goose Lake branch of the Canadian Northern railway, he would use the elevator at Saskatoon, but in the extreme southern part of the province, shipping east, he would also have to go to Moosejaw and use the elevator there if he so desired, because it means a back haul to ship to Calgary.
I understand that the minister maintains that the elevator at Calgary was intended solely for shipments westward, that is by the Pacific. If that was the reason, an elevator could have been located at the city of Lethbridge, which would have served the shipments east to Fort William, and, at the same time, have served shipments west by the Pacific. But the Government insisted on having that elevator for the province of Alberta located at Calgary where it could not.possibly serve for some time shipments to the Pacific coast. That elevator was constructed and placed in operation before the Panama route was opened, before it was even declared feasible for grain shipments. It was placed there solely for the purpose of handling shipments by the Pacific when there was no guarantee that shipments could be made by that particular route. I think that the Government can be charged with making a fatal error in the location of that elevator in the province of Alberta. I am going to use the name of my own city not for selfish reasons, but because I believe that the location of that elevator at Lethbridge would have served shipments east and shipments west. The city of Lethbridge is practically the centre' of the wheat growing area in the extreme southern part of the province of Alberta, and in that extreme southern part I think it can be safely said that 80 per cent of the wheat raised in Alberta is produced. All the railroads run into Lethbridge. The farmers could have shipped their grain there and used the internal elevator at Lethbridge, and it would not have meant a back haul, whereas, to use the elevator at Calgary, under ordinary conditions, means a back haul for the farmers of a great proportion of the wheatgrowing section of the province of Alberta. I asked how much grain the Calgary elevator had handled from the date of the opening till December 31, 1915, and the answer was that the total amount, including all grains, was 185,455 bushels. Then I asked how much the elevator had handled from 1st January to the 14th January in this year, and the answer was that the total amount handled was 248,367 bushels. This elevator has a capacity, according to the minister, of 2,500,000 bushels. That was all the grain that was sent to the elevator up to the 14th January. I admit that since that time there has been a considerably larger amount of grain going into the Calgary elevator. This was not because the location of the elevator warranted the grain going there, but -'because the rates were reduced at the elevator-practically removed-the Canadian Pacific also made a reduction in rates in order to get the grain into the elevator, and an embargo was placed upon grain going out of Alberta to eastern points. All of these things forced the grain into the Calgary elevator. But that was an unnatural condition, due to the action of the railways and to that of the Grain Commission in reducing rates-. My charge against the Government is that this elevator was located at a most undesirable place with reference to the wheat-raising area of Alberta, when it was placed at -Calgary. It should have been placed in the extreme southern part of the province, and it might then have served 80 per cent of the grain-raising parts of the province for shipments east and west. The elevator was placed at Calgary, I believe, against the best judgment of the Grain Commission. I believe it was placed there for purely political reasons, and on account of the patronage system whioh my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce -has condemned, and which I condemn-. I believe that if the constituency which I represent had been represented by a supporter of the Government the elevator would have been placed in that constituency. An argument can be presented in favour of the location of an elevator in that constituency, but there can be no argument in favour of the location of such an elevator at Calgary, except on the theory that it isi intended to serve the western

route. But the western route is not in existence at the present time. I would like the minister to state to-night how much grain has been shipped by the western route during the last twelve months. The shipments are going east and will go east until the conditions warrant them going west, or until it is established that the Panama route can be used, or until we have a market in the far East. I think the minister has learned of the opinion of the farmers in Alberta. I asked a question later on this session as to whether he had received any representation from farmers in Alberta about another elevator in that province. The minister stated that he had received a great many petitions signed by farmers asking that an elevator be placed at the city of Lethbridge in the southern part of Alberta. He knows that the opinion of the farmers is that an elevator should be placed there. I doubt very much whether the Government ever had representations of any kind from any organization of farmers, or from any individual farmers, in favour of locating the elevator at Calgary. I think I have given good reasons why the elevator should have been placed in the southern part of the province, and in support of my argument that it was a mistake to locate the elevator at Calgary. If the minister has any other reasons for the decision of the Government to place the elevator at Calgary, I would like to hear them during the course of this discussion.

If my hon.
friends from,the West who are interested particularly in the question are through, I do not want to do them the discourtesy, nor myself the disadvantage, of not replying to some of the points that were raised by each. Two of the most ingenious things I have heard put forward to-night were put forward by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff). He evolved an absolutely new idea-I do not know whether he has patented it or not-as to why we were talking about the commandeering of grain and about western grain conditions in the House to-night, and the brilliant conclusion at which he arrived was that the Minister of Trade and Commerce was anxious to kill time-so he brought this up. I do not think I have to do more than to mention that to show the extreme ingenuity of my hon. friend and to indicate on what very slight grounds he can build such a substantial structure as he has set up. Then again, he was still more ingenious, if possible, in

another way. In spite of the arguments that he had brought forward, he felt still that his case was weak and so he made it as strong as possible by his final argument along that line. He said that we would do nothing for the farmers, we would not give them back their wheat, and then he thought it a brilliant idea to couple the Ontario millers with the western farmers' wheat. We would not do anything for these small millers he said, but we would fill up the elevators of the big millers in Ontario. I may tell my hon. friend that if he will come to my office to-morrow morning I will be very pleased to show him a list of the mills in Ontario, under exactly the conditions that he has spoken of this afternoon, which required very small amounts of grain to keep them going. The large portion of the grain that was released to the millers of Ontario was released to the men who wanted 10,000, 20,000 or 40,000 bushels to keep their mills going to bread their districts and carry out the obligations they had entered into to deliver flour to their clientele from week to week and month to month. That disposes, I think, pretty well of the two famous arguments of my hon. friend which he evolved like an Egyptian wizard out of nothingness, so to speak. But then he had another idea. If a man receives a definite, positive order, to buy wheat to a certain extent, to be delivered at a certain time, that time being as early in December or even .in November as possible, then, instead of buying it on that order, he should go into the option business and buy options for the succeeding months. In that way he might get the wheat a little cheaper and do something for his clients. But the unfortunate part of the argument is that the client did not want a December or a January option bought. The client wanted wheat bought at a certain time and in certaih quantities. My hon. friend knows that if you buy a December option, the possibilities are that you will not get your wheat until the very last day of December. You run that risk anyway, and a man takes advantage of his option with the idea that he may make something by carrying it to the very last day. Suppose we had bought December options and that at the end of December we had 10,000,000 or 12,000,000 bushels, how would we have brought that out and where would it have been at the present time? I do not think that my hon. friend's suggestion was a very good one.

The hon. member for Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) made 'certain remarks. If my hon. friend had been here wheal I made my remarks immediately after we went into Supply, he would quite well have understood that I did not claim for myself as minister of the department, nor for the Government, all the credit or even a very large part of the credit, for the enactments which now form the Canada Grain Act. If my hon. friend will read Hansard when it comes out to-morrow, he will find that I expressly mentioned the preceding legislation and what had been done, and stated that the legislation of 1912 was a re-construction or reaffirmation, with certain added features, of the legislation which had already been on the statute book or prepared for enactment. 1 was not trying to take the credit for that Act in its entirety or even in great part to the present Government; I did not pursue the argument along that line. What I did say was that some new features were introduced that were important, and I then went on to point them out.
My hon. friend from Regina (Mr. W. M. Martin) stated that the Vancouver elevator was placed there absolutely .as a matter of party patronage. I probably know as much about the Vancouver elevator as my hon. friend does, and, if I had listened particularly to the voice of party patronage, mighty strongly impressed upon me, the elevator would probably not have been at Vancouver to-day, but at some other place. There was, from beginning to end, no thought of party patronage in the placing of that elevator. Rightly or wrongly, we started out with the idea that when the Panama canal was constructed there would be a very available route open all the year round for the passage of the increased production of wheat and other grain in the Northwest toy Vancouver, through that canal, and so on to>
Europe. And so I believe it will come. I have faith in that route, or I would not have helped to have an elevator placed either at Calgary or at Vancouver. I believe that will be a great grain route in the future. It has this advantage, that where one side of Canada is blocked, so fax as ocean traffic conditions are concerned, for a large part of the year, there you have an outlet to the Pacific ocean for whatever may develop in the far East and for the Panama canal trade, and that outlet is open every day in ther yeair. The Vancouver elevator was placed where
it is as the complement of that policy which we had designed and which we were carrying out. That policy may have been a wrong policy or may not, but the Vancouver elevator went as a sequence of that policy, and as an attachment, as it were, to the Calgary elevator.
A suggestion was made that maybe the trouble with reference to the grain arose because it had not been returned either by the parties who had borrowed it or by the parties to whom it had been released or who were exporting wheat to the Old Country. I think I stated this afternoon that every bushel of that grain had been returned, and it was returned absolutely on time as stipulated, in some cases earlier than the time stipulated, so that there was nothing that took place in those two transactions that was not according to the conditions that were imposed and honourably carried out. Furthermore, there is not a bushel of that grain now in western elevators; all of it is in the East waiting for the vessels that are to take it out.
My toon, friend from Medicine Hat (Mr. Buchanan) had something to say with reference to the location of the elevator as between Calgary and Lethbridge. In so far as he gave the facts with regard to petitions and to grain production, he stated them exactly as they are. Lethbridge is a large grain centre. A wonderful transformation has taken place in southern Alberta; that country, which a few years ago, it was supposed, was not worth five cents for 'grain, and would all have to go to grazing and cattle and stock raising, suddenly developed into a great grain-producing district that astonished even the people of Lethbridge and of that part of Alberta, and for the last few years at least has produced large quantities of grain. My hon. Ifriend is exactly right when he says that the southern part of Alberta would find Lethbridge very much in its line for shipments east; but it also finds Moosejaw in its line for shipments east, the elevator at Moosejaw being available for that purpose. For shipments east it has little, if any, use for the Calgary elevator. But that elevator was meant for shipments west, not for shipments east, and was built partly as a feeder to the transfer elevator which was afterwards to be erected at Vancouver.
At least two of my hon. friends have broken out into the strongest arguments against internal storage elevators generally. My hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver)

.said that instead of spending the money for one or any or all of these internal storage elevators, the money should have been expended to put up elevators at St. John, Halifax and Quebec, and he developed his argument that if we only had had elevators there last year, great good would have been accomplished. I think I made it as plain as could be when I spoke here a day <jr two ago, and I think I made it plain again to-day; but, if not, I will make it plain now, that if you had had all the storage capacity of the three elevators at Moose-jaw, Saskatoon and Calgary, down either in Quebec or St. John or Halifax, or distributed between them, you would not have got one bushel more of western wheat on to the markets and into consumption in Europe than you have this year without those storage elevators there. I do not want to be misunderstood, in that. I believe that a port like Montreal should have pretty large storage facilities, and a port like Quebec should also have good storage facilities, because they are both transfer positions; but there is an advantage to have at those two points, in readiness for the spring opening of transport out by the Atlantic, large storage facilities, so that whatever can be carried down of the surplus of wheat during the winter season by the railways will find a resting place there and be ready for the spring opening. The conditions, however, this year were such with regard to transport by the ocean that no amount of storage at those ports would have helped the Atlantic situation to any extent. Do not let us be too hard on those storage elevators in the West. They were not built tor one year or two years; they were built for permanent use. Things are in their growing condition in the West. Closer farming conditions, greater additions to the wheat-producing area, will be constantly going on in the West, and I believe that these storage elevators perform a good office at the present time and will more and more come to commend themselves and prove beneficial to the wheatgrowing interests in their districts, but even up to the present time they have not done so badly. I ask the attention of my hon. friend to the Calgary elevator. He has stated-and it is to some extent true-that extraordinary conditions this year have drawn more wheat into Calgary than might come under different conditions. The Calgary elevator, up to a late date, had received 1,729,916 bushels, and shipped 352,720 bushels-a movement of a [Sir George Foster.}
little over two million bushels. The Saskatoon elevator has received 6,841,874 bushels of grain, and has shipped out.
4,274,000	bushels!-over eleven million bushels have passed in and out of that elevator this year, and the work is still going on. As to Mooisejaw, unfortunately I have not the exact figures, but I think it has had a movement of close upon eight millions of bushels of grain, this season up to the present time. True, this is an abnormal year. But it is well t.o have some provision for abnormal years. This year has been abnormal in the greatness of production, but we had an abnormal year once when bad weather and other unfavourable conditions caused a deterioration of a vast amount of grain. In james like either of these, these elevators will save millions of dollars to the grain-producing interests of the West. So, even if they have to depend for full action upon abnormal conditions yet, year in and year out, they will satisfy,
I am sure, a certain, want in that country, and will prove very useful in their day- and I hope their day will be a long one. Other remarks were made by my hon. friend, but I am sure that both of us are pretty well agreed that iwe have talked long enough and killed enough time on this ' particular phase of the discussion.

I understood the minister to state that if the Alberta elevator had been located at Lethbridge it would have served shipments east only, meaning that it * would not have served shipments west. And he said that the elevator at Calgary is of no service for shipments east, meaning that it was intended only for shipments west. But I contend that if the elevator had been located at Lethbridge it would have served shipments west even better than at Calgary, and at the same time would have served shipments east, which the Calgary elevator cannot do. Lethbridge is on the Crowsnest branch of the Canadian Pacific. The company has constructed a branch from the Crowsnest line through the Windermere vialley to Golden, on the Canadian Pacific, reducing both the grade and the mileage, and giving a through route by the Crowsnest Pass and the Windermere valley to Vancouver and other Pacific ports. With such a location Lethbridge would have been a better place for the elevator as a means of serving western shipments than Calgary, and it would have 'been in a position to serve shipments east also. Another thing

to be remembered is that the Canadian Pacific is building practically another through' line from Winnipeg and Lethbridge to the coast, known as the Lethbridge-Weyburn line, opening a large country in the southern part of Alberta. All the grain could go west if desired, and if shipment east was desired it could go as well by that route as by the main line. Besides that, Lethbridge is in the heart of the wheat growing section of Aloerta. When you go north to Ualgary you are in an area where mixed farming almost wholly prevails, and from which hardly any shipments of grain are made. South of Calgary it is almost purely wheat raising country. I think the minister is wrong in stating that the Alberta elevator if located at Lethbridge would have served the east almost wholly. It would serve the west as well as Calgary, but would have served both, and not the west only.

The day before yesterday I was in the beginning of asking the minister for information in regard to the grain situation: first, in relation to the 11,000,000 bushels transported over the Transcontinental, and then, generally, the situation of the grain in the country-how much of the total crop was sold in the country and where it was located, and how, much had gone across the ocean? I think the minister said that the question might well have been discussed at that time, but that he would be ready on another occasion when the item was under discussion to give the information. If he has the -information, I shall be glad if he will give it to me.

As to the 11,000,000 bushels hauled over the Transcontinental, I am not able to give my hon. friend the information as to where that lies or how it was distributed. But I have not forgotten that I said I would try to get that information, and I will get it if the Minister of Railways/ who also promised the information, does not get it. At any rate, we will have the information here on Monday. As to the other, speaking generally, if my memory serves me well a bulletin was issued last week by the statistical branch of my department which gave about the location, within a very short time, of the grain in the country. I cannot remember exactly the quantities, but I think that at the head of the lakes

I remember, there were
50.000.	000 bushels of all grains at the head of the lakes on the 14th of April.

I have information here that is rather interesting bearing somewhat on the subject referred to. The Dominion elevator at Port Arthur received this season 19,600,000 bushels, and made shipments" of 16,619,000, up to April 14, 1916. That is, it handled, in and out, about
36.000.	000 bushels of grain. The terminals at Fort William had receipts of 228,000,000 bushels of grain, and handled out 190,000,000 bushels of grain.
Grain or wheat?

That is all grains. Wheat was shipped from Fort William to United States lake ports, 77,800,000 bushels to Buffalo and 20,700,000 to the other United States ports on the lake, making altogether
98.500.000.	To the Canadian lake ports 4)1,-
800,000	bushels were shipped, and to Montreal 823,271, a total of 42,600,000 bushels. That is to say, during the last season 70 per cent of the grain went out via Buffalo and nearby United States ports, according to that calculation. I find that 63 per cent of the 183,365 cars that were inspected, embracing a -little over 300,000,000 bushels, graded No. 1 northern and better, and 80
per cent graded No. 3 northern
10 p.m. and better. That was an extraordinary showing for the crop of wheat in the West this year. This year, with its quality as well as its quantity, the grain of Canada, particularly that of the Northwest, has made a name throughout Europe, especially among the allied nations, that will be very beneficial in future transactions. The British, French and Italian Governments have all been pleased with the quality of the grain that they have got. As I mentioned in the committee once before, it is vastly superior to the quality of the wheat from the United States. I do not mean to say that they have not a quantity of very superior wheat, but the quality of their wheat this year does not in excellence grade up to ours.

The fact is-without desiring to give the hon. minister information in regard to his own business-that the United States- does not export its best wheat, while Canada does.
Sir GEORGE- FOSTER: It exports some of its best wheat
That is why they want free trade.
1 am afraid I have not the particular information that my hon. friend asks for, but I will be sure to get it.
What is. the estimated total production of wheat in .the three Prairie Provinces last year?

Up to the end of October 15, 1915, the total production for Canada was estimated at 336,258,000 bushels, of which the Northwest Provinces pro; duced 304,2010,000 bushels'. Of oats, the total for Canada was 480,000,000, in round figures; the Northwest Provinces produced 305,000,000. Of barley, the total for Canada was 50,800,000; the North-west produced 33,000,000. Of flax, the total for Canada was 12,604,700, of which the Northwest Provinces produced 12,537,000.

Of this total production of
304.000.	000, only 139,000,000 bushels are accounted for as having passed east of Fort William?

My impression
just now is that the estimates that passed through my office the other day gave about
80.000.	000 as still in the farmers' hands.
Of courses, there is a good deal in the interior elevators.
Yes'.

Then my figure is correct, is it not; 97,000,000 to United States points and 42,000,000 to Canadian points makes
139.000.	000 in all?

That is about
what it was.
That would leave a little over half the crop, more than 150,000,000 bushels still west of the lakes?

The estimate
might be a little large now; it is coming out pretty rapidly.
Is there any estimate of the amount required for local seed and feed?

I have not the
estimate here, and I would not like to make the calculation. I will send my hon. friend the information.

I find, according to my
account here, that over 160,000,000 bushels were still west of the lakes on the 14th of

April. Deducting 20,000,000 for seed and bread, that leaves 140,000,000 still for export. Of the 142,000,000 that went forward east, 97,000,000 went to United States ports. Of the 42,000,000 that went forward to eastern ports, how much crossed the ocean during the period from October 15 to April 14?

I will have a
statement made out and see that my hon. friend gets it. I am not able to give it tonight.

What I want to know is how much wheat passing through Canadian ports has crossed the ocean since the first of October, 1915, in order that one may judge approximately what the prospects are for getting tonnage to carry the balance of our export surplus, which we desire to dispose of before our next crop becomes available.
As against the $725,000 expended in connection with the running of the whole grain business, what were the receipts from inspections and general revenue under the Grain Act?

The revenue
that is derived, as my hon. friend knows, comes from the car inspection fee of 50 cents for each car; the weighing fee of 30 cents for each car; the in-registration fee, when the car goes into the elevator of 4 cents; and the cancellation fee of 4 cents. Those added together amount to 88 cents. That is what might be called the actual fees in connection with the administration of the Act. The other revenue is really earnings, that is for service given, such as might 1 be given by a private elevator owner. At the terminal elevator at Port Arthur, for instance, there are the following items:	storage, $159,518; cleaning,
$4,994; drying, $8,299; bulkheads, a small amount; sale of screenings, $24,000. Then there are some other smaller items. You must add to or subtract from that revenue the overage or shortage at the end of the year. In our own elevatoF we had an overage in flax to the value of $26,816. I made particular inquiry as to how we came to have that overage, and the commission informed me that that overage in flax is due to the very fine methods employed in screening it and getting out from what is in other elevators waste, real value. At the Saskatoon elevator some of the items of revenue were: storage, $46,575; cleaning, $20,604; drying, a small amount; screenings, $1,000; grinding screenings, $2,686; packing

for the seed grain, $12,268. The total revenue from that particular elevator was $91,453.
If my hon. friend would give me the total revenues.
I have not them made up. That, however, gives the sources of the earnings.
Has the minister any record of shipments of wheat by the western ports last year?

I do not think
there were any large shipments of grain via Vancouver. Some grain did go west for Japan and South America, and there may have been some other for the far East, but it was a small quantity .A considerable shipment was put through for New Zealand. A portion of the grain purchased for New Zealand was shipped via Vancouver and went through, having been sacked at our elevator at Moosejaw. As my hon. friend knows, not only was traffic through the Panama canal' disorganized by the war, but the Panama canal itself has been closed for months on account of land slides.

Does the minister
know whether it will be possible to ship grain via the Panama canal without sacking at Vancouver?

Of course you
can never be positive about anything until you have made the experiment, but if grain can be shipped from the Argentine to London, passing through the tropical belt without harm, I do not see why the short passage through the Panama canal should injure grain in good condition. That is the impression of some of the best grain men.

Could the minister give
me the annual consumption and production of wheat in Canada east of the Lakes?

I have not the
figures here, but I can send my hon. friend the whole statement in print. I would refer my hon. friend to the monthly bulletin of statistics published by the department.

I do not think that the
figures I have asked for are contained in the very interesting statistics published in the bulletin.

I suppose we can never get at the exact consumption of grain in the East or West. You have to make an estimate, and generally it is estimated that
about six bushels to the head is a generous consumption.

The situation as to general transportation seems to me to be very serious. About 42,000,000 bushels of grain has come to eastern Canadian ports. A large proportion of that will necessarily be for local consumption. If one-quarter of it was for local consumption, that would leave us with 30,000,000 bushels seeking ocean transport, and the information the minister has given to the House is to the effect that it has not been able to secure ocean transport. If that is the result of the transport business for six months, what is going to happen to us when we have to get rid of
140,000,000 bushels in the succeeding six months?

Of course, a

The hon. member has put a very large question to me, but there is one method of solution; let us try, a!1 of us, to do the best we can to raise as many more mouths as possible to take care of the extra consumption.

The minister has been giving us lots of information to-night, and I would like some more before we arise. Is it the intention of the Government to establish more than one storage elevator in the province of Alberta? That is all I ask; 1 will not ask where it is to be placed.

I will tell my hon. friend this: I have had a great number of petitions, and a good deal of correspondence, and I have .taken the position that the elevators that we have already built-at Saskatoon and Mbosejaw-in connection with the east, and the Hudson bay transfer elevator on the northern route, when it is opened, together with the terminal elevator at the head of the lakes, complete what was in our minds at the time when the policy was laid down.



Then the Calgary elevator, with the transfer elevator at Vancouver, completes that end of the policy. It was not part of that policy that we should erect interior storage elevators in the West wherever they might be useful. I know that that is quite an easy road for the man who wants storage to travel on. He says: Here is a district which has much more production than storage capacity; you have a storage elevator at Moosejaw; why do you not put a storage elevator down here. We are trying to keep on the track of linking up all the storage elevators with the transfer elevators at the ports, and along that line the policy at the present time has been carried out as far as we had anticipated. Even supposing that it was not war time, it would scarcely seem possible for us to anticipate a further expenditure of money for storage facilities, leaving that to corporate and private capital to take up. The Transcontinental railway with the Intercolonial railway having a great service, has to supply certain storage facilities, and more storage facilities are necessary in connection with that road than exist at the present time, so that there will be an extension of Government building-to what extent I do not yet know-in connection with railway transportation. But I suppose that when we cease to hope we cease to live, or to put it the other way, hope on as long a6 you live.
